entry.sense:
ἀάα_τος: in Il. with penult. long,
not to be injured, inviolable, νῦν μοι ὄμοσσον ἀάα_τον Στυγὸς ὕδωρ, because the gods swore their most binding oaths thereby.

ἀάατος: in Od. with penult. short,
hurtful, perilous, aweful; ἄεθλος ἀάατος.
unbroken, not to be broken, hard, strong, Od., Theocr.
not to be touched, resistless, invincible, χεῖρες ἄαπτοι Hom., Hes.
insatiate, c. gen., Ἄρης ἆτος πολέμοιο Il.

entry.etym: The quantities vary: α_ασεν, α_α_σαν, part. ἀασας: ἀ_ασάμην, ἀ_α_σατο: ἀ_ασθην, ἀασθη.
entry.sense:
properly
to hurt, damage; then
to mislead, infatuate, of the effects of wine, sleep, divine judgments, Od.; so in Mid., Ἄτη ἣ πάντας ἀᾶται Il.

aor1 mid. and pass.,
to act recklessly or
foolishly, ἀασάμην
I was infatuated Il.; μέγʼ ἀάσθη id=Il.

entry.etym: epic Verb only used in aor1.
entry.sense: to be speechless, epic Verb only used in aor1, οἱ δʼ ἀβάκησαν πάντες Od.
speechless, infantine, Sapph..

uninitiated in the Bacchic orgies, generally,
joyless, Eur.

properly ἆ βάλε, expressing a wish,
O that! Lat. utinam, c. inf., Anth.
without weight: not burdensome, of persons, NTest.

not examined by torture, untortured; of things,
unexamined, Plut.; adv. -τως,
without examination, Thuc.
not ruled by a king, Thuc., Xen.
not subject to enchantment; adv. -τως, Anth.
not to be carried, Plut.

untrodden, impassable, inaccessible, of mountains, Hdt., Soph., etc.; of a river,
not fordable, Xen.

of holy places,
not to be trodden, like ἄθικτος, Soph.: metaph.
pure, chaste, ψυχή Plat.

of horses,
not ridden, Luc.

act., ἄβ. πόνος a plague
that hinders walking, i.e. gout, Luc.

Hebr. word,
father, NTest.
a man of Abdera in Thrace, proverb. of simpletons. Dem.

like an Abderite, i.e.
stupid, Luc.
uncertain, unsteady; τὸ ἀβέβαιον = ἀβεβαιότης, Luc.

of persons,
unstable, Dem., etc.
not profane, inviolable, Plut.
silliness, stupidity, fatuity, Plat.
good for nothing, silly, stupid, fatuous, Ar., etc.;—Sup. -ώτατος, id=Ar.
unforced, without violence, Plat.
= ἀβίωτος, Anth.
without a living, starving, Luc.

of the Ἱππημολγοί,
simple in life, Il.

not to be lived, insupportable, ἀβ. πεποίηκε τὸν βίον Ar.; ἀβίωτον χρόνον βιοτεῦσαι Eur.; ἀβίωτόν [ἐστι]
life is intolerable, Eur., Plat.; adv., ἀβιώτως ἔχειν to find
life intolerable, Plut.
freedom from harm, Plut.

act.
harmlessness, Lat. innocentia, Cic.
without harm, i.e.,

pass.
unharmed, unhurt, secure, Aesch., etc.

act.
not harming, harmless, innocent, Aesch., Plat.

averting or
preventing harm, Theocr.

adv. in attic formularies, ἀβλαβῶς σπονδαῖς ἐμμένειν
without doing harm, Thuc.; so the σπονδαί themselves are entitled ἄδολοι καὶ ἀβλαβεῖς, id=Thuc.
without eye-lids, Anth.

not thrown or
shot, ἰὸν ἀβλῆτα an arrow
not yet used, Il.
not hit by darts, Il.
without bleatings, Anth.

weak, feeble, Il.; ἀβλ. θάνατος an
easy death in ripe old age, opp. to a
violent one, Od.
of sheep, Babr.
helpless, Plut.
without summons, Pind.
not loudly lamented, Anth.
ungrazed, ὄρη Babr.

untended by herdsmen: metaph.
unheeded, Aesch.

entry.etym: ἀβουλέω is an exception to the rule that α privat. cannot be comp. directly with Verbs.
entry.sense: to be unwilling, Plat.
want of counsel, thoughtlessness, Hdt., Soph., etc.

inconsiderate, ill-advised, Soph., etc.; τέκνοισι ἄβουλος
taking no thought for them, id=Soph.: comp. -ότερος, Thuc.; adv. -ως,
inconsiderately, Hdt.; Sup. ἀβουλότατα, id=Hdt.

without oxen, i.e.
poor, Hes.
of no weight, Eur.

softly or
delicately stepping, Aesch.
living delicately, effeminate, Plut.
wailing womanishly, Aesch.

living delicately, Aesch.; τὸ ἁβροδίαιτον
effeminacy, Thuc.

with delicate or
luxuriant leaves, φοῖνιξ Eur., Anacreont.
without Bacchus, Anth.
noiseless; epith. of the Trojans in Il., v. αὐίαχος.
with soft sandals, Anth.
of delicate texture, Aesch.
richly luxuriant, Eur.

entry.etym: perhaps the same root as ἥβη?
entry.sense:
delicate, graceful, beauteous, pretty, Anacr., etc.: of things,
splendid, Pind.—Very early the word took the notion of
over-delicate, dainty, luxurious; hence neut. as adv. ἁβρὰ παθεῖν to live
delicately, Solon; ἁβρὰ παρηΐδος = ἁβρὰν παρηΐδα, Eur.; ἁβρῶς and ἁβρὸν βαίνειν to step
delicately, id=Eur.

entry.etym: From same Root with ἀμβροτεῖν, ἁμαρτεῖν, μ being rejected.
entry.sense:
to miss, c. gen., only in aor1 subj., μήπως ἀβροτάξομεν (epic for -ωμεν) ἀλλήλοιϊν that
we may not
miss one another, Il.

delicacy, luxury, Pind.; οὐκ ἐν ἁβρότητι κεῖσαι thou art not in a position
to be fastidious, Eur.
delicate and costly, Aesch.

immortal, divine, holy, νὺξ ἀβρότη, either
holy Night, as a divinity, (like ἱερὸν κνέφας, ἱερὸν ἦμαρ), or
never failing (like ἄφθιτος ἠώς), Il.; ἔπη ἄβροτα
holy hymns, Soph.
without men, solitary, Aesch.

in soft tunic, softly clad, Anth.; εὐνὰς ἁβροχίτωνας beds
with soft coverings, Aesch.

unwetted, unmoistened, Aeschin.:
wanting rain, waterless, Eur.

to make delicate, treat delicately, Aesch.:
to deck or
trick out, εἰς γάμον ἁβρῦναί τινα Anth.; Mid. or Pass.
to live delicately; then
to wax wanton, give oneself airs, Aesch.; c. gen. rei,
to pride or
plume oneself on a thing, Eur.
from Abydos, Il.
at Abydos, Il.
Abydos, the town on the Asiatic side of the Hellespont.

with no bottom, bottomless, unfathomed, Hdt.; generally,
unfathomable, enormous, Aesch.

ἡ ἄβυσσος,
the great deep, the abyss, bottomless pit, NTest.
seeming good, Plat.
to do good, NTest.
a good deed, service rendered, Lat. beneficium, Hdt.
doing good: — οἱ Ἀγαθοεργοί, at Sparta, the five oldest and most approved knights, who went on foreign missions for the state, Hdt.

to do good, NTest.; ἀγ. τινά
to do good to, id=NTest.
to do well, act rightly, id=NTest.
well doing, NTest.
doing good, beneficent.
good, Lat. bonus:
of persons,

in early times,
good, gentle, noble, in reference to birth, opp. to κακοί, πατρὸς δʼ εἴμʼ ἀγαθοῖο, θεὰ δέ με γείνατο μήτηρ Il.; ἀγαθοὶ καὶ ἐξ ἀγαθῶν, Lat. boni bonis prognati, Plat.; with this early sense was associated that of wealth and power, like Lat. optimus quisque in Sallust and Cicero; esp. in the phrase καλοὶ κἀγαθοί (v. καλοκἀγαθός).

good, brave, since these qualities were attributed to the Chiefs, Il.; ἀγαθὸς ἐν ὑσμίνῃ, βοὴν ἀγαθός, πὺξ ἀγαθός, etc., Hom.; ἀγ. τὰ πολέμια, τὰ πολιτικά Hdt., etc.;—also c. dat., ἀγ. πολέμῳ Xen.;—and, ἀγ. εἴς τι, περί τι, πρός τι Plat., etc.; lastly, c. inf., ἀγ. μάχεσθαι, ἱππεύεσθαι,
good at fighting, etc., Hdt.
good, in moral sense, Plat., etc.
ἀγαθοῦ δαίμονος, as a toast, "to the good Genius," Ar.
of things,

good, serviceable, Ἰθάκη ἀγαθὴ κουροτρόφος Od.; ἀγ. τοῖς τοκεῦσι, τῇ πόλει Xen.; c. gen., εἴ τι οἶδα πυρετοῦ ἀγ.
good for fever, id=Xen.; ἀγαθόν [ἐστι], c. inf.,
it is good to do so and so, Hom., etc.

ἀγαθόν, τό,
a good, of persons, φίλον, ὃ μέγιστον ἀγ. εἶναι φασι Xen.; ἐπʼ ἀγαθῷ τοῖς πολίταις Ar.; τὸ ἀγαθόν or τἀγαθόν,
the good, summum bonum, Plat., etc.; in pl., ἀγαθά, τά,
the goods of fortune, wealth, Hdt., etc.; also
good qualities, of a horse, Xen.

instead of the
regular degrees of comparison, many forms are used,—comp. ἀμείνων, ἀρείων, βελτίων, κρείσσων, λωΐων , epic βέλτερος, λωΐτερος, φέρτερος; — Sup. ἄριστος, βέλτιστος, κράτιστος, λώϊστος, epic βέλτατος, κάρτιστος, φέρτατος, φέριστος.
the adv. is usually εὖ: ἀγαθῶς in late writers.
goodness, kindness, NTest.

entry.etym: epic and ionic for ἄγαμαι, only in pres. and in bad sense (cf. ἄγη II).
entry.sense:
c. gen. rei,
to be indignant at, Od.

c. dat. pers.
to be indignant with, Hdt.
very glorious, famous, Lat. inclytus, Il., Pind.
= ἀγακλεής, Hom., etc.
of things, ἀγακλειτὴ ἑκατόμβη Od.
Lat. inclytus, of men, Hom., Hes.
of things, Od.

well-built or
placed, πόλις Pind.

without milk, getting no milk, i.e.
taken from the mother's breast, Horace's
jam lacte depulsus, Aesch.
great joy, exultation, NTest.
to rejoice exceedingly, NTest.

the iris or
flag, Hhymn.

entry.etym: Pass., mostly in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense:
to make glorious, glorify, exalt, c. acc. : esp.
to pay honour to a god, ἀγ. τινὰ θυσίαισι Ar.;
to adorn, deck, γαμηλίους εὐνάς Eur.; Pass.
to glory, take delight, exult in a thing, c. dat., Hom., attic; absol., Hdt., etc.

a glory, delight, honour, Il., attic; ἀγάλματʼ ἀγορᾶς
mere ornaments of the agora, Eur.
a pleasing gift, esp. for the gods, Od.

a statue in honour of a god, Hdt., attic;
an image, as an object of worship, etc., Aesch.; then generally,= ἀνδριάς,
any statue, Plat.: also
a portrait, picture, ἐξαλειφθεῖσʼ ὡς ἄγαλμα Eur.
a maker of statues, a sculptor, statuary, Hdt., Plat., etc.

absol.
to wonder, be astonished, Hom.

c. acc.
to admire a person or thing, id=Hom., Hdt.; so in attic, ταῦτα ἀγασθείς Xen.; c. acc. pers. et rei,
to admire one
for a thing, Plat., Xen.

c. gen. rei only, often in Com.,
to wonder at, λόγων Ar.

c. acc. rei et gen. pers., οὐκ ἄγαμαι ταῦτʼ ἀνδρός
I admire not this in a man, Eur.

c. gen. pers., foll. by a part.,
to wonder at one's doing, ἀγ. αὐτοῦ εἰπόντος Plat.

c. dat.
to be delighted with a person or thing, Hdt., Eur., etc.

in bad sense,
to feel envy, bear a grudge against a person, c. dat., Hom.

c. acc.
to be jealous or
angry at a thing, Od. Cf. ἀγαίομαι.

of or
having to do with Agamemnon, Hom., Pind., Aesch.
Agamemnon's son, Orestes, Od.
the very steadfast, name of the leader of the Greeks against Troy, Hom.

part. pres. of ἄγαμαι,
with admiration, respect or
deference, Plat.
celibacy, Plut.; ἀγαμίου δίκη, ἡ, an action against one for not marrying, Plut.
unmarried, unwedded, single, Lat. caelebs, Il., Trag.

γάμος ἄγαμος,
a marriage that is no marriage, a fatal marriage, Soph., Eur.

to feel irritation: metaph.
to be vexed, annoyed, angry, discontented, Ar., Plat.; c. dat. rei,
to be vexed at a thing, id=Plat.; ἐπί τινι Isocr., ὑπέρ τινος, διά τι Plat.

to be vexed at or
with a person, τινί Xen.; πρός τινα Plut.; κατά τινος Luc.: c. acc. pers., ἀγ. τινὰς ἀποθνήσκοντας
to be angry at their dying, Plat.

irritation, of the irritation caused by teething, Plat.: metaph., ἀγανάκτησιν ἔχει the thing gives
ground for annoyance or
displeasure, Thuc.
irritable, Plat.
irritating, Plat.
much snowed on, snow-capt, Il.
mild-eyed, Anth.

mild, gentle, kindly, of words, Hom., Pind.; in Hom. of the shafts of Apollo and Artemis, as
bringing an easy death; Sup. ἀγανώτατος, Hes.: adv. -νῶς, Eur.
gentleness, kindliness, Hom.

poet. adj.
gentle of mood, Hom.

entry.etym: ἄγα_ν properly, but ἄγαν in Anth.
entry.sense:
very, much, very much, Theogn., Attic, the word λίην being its equiv. in epic and ionic: in bad sense,
too, too much, Lat. nimis, as in the famous μηδὲν ἄγαν,
ne quid nimis, not
too much of any thing, Theogn., etc.
admiring, Hes.

to treat with affection, shew affection to a person,
caress, c. acc., Hom.; so in Mid., Od.

of persons,
to treat with affection, to caress, love, be fond of, c. acc., attic for ἀγαπάζω, Plat., etc.; Pass.
to be beloved, id=Plat., Dem.

in NTest.
to regard with brotherly love, v. ἀγαπή.

of things,
to be well pleased or
contented at or
with a thing, c. dat., Dem., etc.; also c. acc. rei, id=Dem.; absol.
to be content, Luc.: —ἀγ. ὅτι.., εἰ.., ἐὰν..,
to be well pleased that . . ., Thuc., etc.
a delight, darling, Anth.

= ἠνορέην ἀγαπῶν,
loving manliness, manly, Il.

love: esp.
brotherly love, charity; the love of God for man and of man for God, NTest.

in pl.
a love-feast, id=NTest.
to be loved, desired, Plat.
affectionate, Plut.

beloved, of an
only son, Hom., Dem.

of things,
worthy of love, loveable, dear, Plat., etc.

to be acquiesced in (as the least in a choice of evils), ἀγαπητόν [ἐστι]
one must be content, εἰ.., ἐάν.., id=Plat., Xen., etc.

adv. -τῶς,
cheerfully, contentedly, Plat., Dem., etc.
just enough to content one, only just, barely, scarcely, Plat.
strong-flowing, swift-flowing, Il.

much groaning, howling, of waves, Od.:
loud-wailing, Aesch.

entry.etym: ἀγατός poet. for ἀγαστός, as θαυματός for θαυμαστός, Hhymn.; verb. adj. of ἄγαμαι
entry.sense:
deserving admiration, later form of the Hom. ἀγητός,
admirable, Eur., Xen.; adv. -τῶς, id=Xen. poet. for ἀγαστός, as θαυματός for θαυμαστός, Hhymn.
illustrious, noble, Hom.; Sup. -ότατος, Od.
stately, proud, Hes.: superl. adv. ἀγαυρότατα, Hdt.

to press one
to serve as a courier, to press into service, NTest.
ἀγγαρήϊος, Ionic form of ἄγγαρος, Hdt.

neut. ἀγγαρήϊον,
post-riding, the Persian system of mounted couriers, id=Hdt.

Persian word,
a mounted courier, such as were kept ready at regular stages throughout Persia for carrying the royal despatches; cf. ἀγγαρήϊος, and v. Xen. Cyr. 8. 6, 17.

as adj., ἄγγαρον πῦρ the
courier flame, said of beacon fires used for telegraphing, Aesch.

a message, tidings, news, Hom., Hdt., etc.; ἀγγελίη ἐμή
a report of me,
concerning me, Il.; ἀγγελίην πατρὸς φέρει ἐρχομένοιο he brings
news of or
about thy father's coming, Od.: — ἀγγελίην ἐλθεῖν, to go
a message, i. e.
on a message, like Lat. legationem obire, Il.;—so also epic in gen., ἀγγελίης οἴχνεσκε went
on account of a message, id=Od.; ἤλυθε σεῦ ἕνεκʼ ἀγγελίης ( i. e. ἀγγελίης σοῦ ἕνεκα) id=Od., Hes.
a proclamation, command, Hhymn., etc.

a messenger, Hdt.: title of
the Persian minister who introduced people to the king, id=Hdt.

to bear a message, τινί
to a person, Hom.; c. acc. et inf.
to make proclamation that, Il.

c. acc. rei,
to announce, proclaim, report, Hom., attic

c. acc. pers.
to bring news of, Od.; περί τινος Soph.

Mid.
to announce oneself, id=Soph.

Pass.
to be reported of, id=Soph., etc.; τὰ ἠγγελμένα
the reports, Thuc.
a message, tidings, news, Eur., Thuc., etc.
a messenger, envoy, Hom., Hdt., attic

generally,
one that announces, of birds of augury, Il.; Μουσῶν ἄγγελος, of a poet, Theogn.; Διὸς ἄγγ., of the nightingale, Soph.; c. gen. rei, ἄγγ. κακῶν ἐμῶν id=Soph.
a divine messenger, an angel, NTest.

a vessel of various kinds,
a jar to hold milk, etc., Hom.:
a vat for the vintage, Hes.;
a vase, pitcher, pail, Hdt., attic

a coffer or
ark, in which children were laid, Hdt., Eur.:
a chest for clothes, Soph.:
a cinerary urn, id=Soph.
the cell of a honeycomb, Anth.

to bring together, gather together, c. acc., Hom., attic; Pass.
to come together, gather, assemble, Hom.; ἀγρόμενοι σύες
herded swine, Od.; θυμὸς ἐνὶ στήθεσσιν ἀγέρθη, ἐς φρένα θυμὸς ἀγέρθη Il.

of things,
to get together, collect, gather, Od.; so in Mid., id=Od.
to collect by begging, id=Od.

ὀφρύας εἰς ἓν ἀγείρειν
to frown, Anth.

without neighbour, neighbourless, Aesch.; φίλων ἀγ.
with no friends
as neighbours, Eur.
belonging to a herd, feeding at large, Hom., attic.

in herds or
shoals, gregarious, ἰχθύες Hdt.; ἀγελαῖα, τά,
gregarious animals, Plat.

of the herd or
multitude, i.e.
common, id=Plat., etc.
to lead a company, c. gen., Plut.
the leader of a company, captain, Plut., Luc.
without laughter, Plut.
not laughing, grave, gloomy, sullen, Hhymn., Aesch.

pass.
not to be laughed at, not trifling, id=Aesch.

epic epith. of Athena,
driver of spoil, forager, Il.

in herds or
companies, Il., Hdt.:— doric ἀγελα_δόν, Theocr.
a herd, of horses, of oxen and kine, cf. βούνομος; of swine, Hes.

any herd or
company, Soph., Eur.; metaph., πόνων ἀγέλαι id=Eur.
of unrecorded descent, NTest.

beardless; ἀγένειόν τι εἰρηκέναι to speak
like a boy, Luc.
unborn, uncreated, unoriginated, Plat.

of things,
not done, not having happened, ἀγένητον ποιεῖν, Lat. infectum reddere, Soph.
of no family, low-born, Hdt., Plat., etc.
low-minded, Hdt., Ar., etc.

of things, much like βάναυσος,
illiberal, sordid, Plat.; adv. -νῶς, Eur.
unbegotten, unborn, ἀγ. τότʼ ἦ Soph.

like ἀγεννής,
low-born, id=Soph.

nearest, next, c. gen., Hdt.; ἀγχ. τινός
very near, i. e.
very like, some one, id=Hdt.; also τινί id=Hdt.:— οἱ ἀγχοτάτω προσήκοντες
the nearest of kin, id=Hdt.:— so, ἀγχότατα ἔχειν τινός
to be most like one, id=Hdt.

comp. of ἀγχοῦ,
nearer, c. gen., Hdt.

= ἄγχι,
near, nigh, ἀγχοῦ δʼ ἱσταμένη Hom.;c. gen. id=Hom., Hdt.
neighbouring, Anth.

nearly equal, ἀγχώμαλοι ἐν χειροτονίᾳ Thuc.; ἀγχ. μάχη a
doubtful battle, id=Thuc.: — as adv., ἀγχώμαλα ναυμαχεῖν, Lat. aequo Marte pugnare, id=Thuc. adv. -λως, Luc.

to compress, press tight, esp. the throat,
to strangle, throttle, choke, ἄγχε μιν ἱμὰς ὑπὸ δειρήν Il.; τὸν Κέρβερον ἀπῇξας ἄγχων Ar.: metaph. of creditors, id=Ar., NTest.; of a guilty conscience, τοῦτο ἄγχει Dem.
fit for leading by, of a dog's leash, Anth.

one that draws or
drags, Hdt.
a leading-rein, leash, Soph., Xen.
a carrying away, carriage, Hdt., etc.; πρὸς τὰς ἀγωγὰς χρῆσθαι ὑποζυγίοις Plat.

intr., τὴν ἀγωγὴν ἐποιεῖτο pursued his
voyage, Thuc.:
movement, τοῦ ποδός Plat.

a bringing to or
in, ὑμῶν ἡ ἐς τοὺς ὀλίγους ἀγ. your
bringing us
before the council, Thuc.
a carrying off, abduction, Aesch., Soph.

a leading towards a point,
guiding, ἵππου Xen.

the leading of an army, Plat.; ἐν ταῖς ἀγ. on
marches, Xen.

a training, education, Plat., etc.; of plants,
culture, Theophr.

easy to be led or
carried, τρισσῶν ἁμαξῶν ἀγώγιμον βάρος weight
enough to load three wains, Eur.; τὰ ἀγώγιμα
things portable, wares, Xen., etc.

of persons,
to be carried off, delivered into bondage, Dem.
easily led, complaisant, Plut.
the load of a wagon, Xen.

leading, and as Subst.
a guide, Hdt., etc.: c. gen., δύναμις ἀνθρώπων ἀγωγός power
of leading men, Plut.
leading towards a point, εἴς, πρός or ἐπί τι Plat., etc.
drawing forth, eliciting, χοαὶ νεκρῶν ἀγωγοί Eur.; δακρύων ἀγ. id=Eur.

absol.
attractive, Plut.
judge of a contest, Soph.

a contest, struggle for victory, διὰ πάσης ἀγωνίης ἔχειν to embrace every kind
of contest, Hdt.; πολεμίων ἀγωνία Eur.; ἐν δημοτικῇ ἀγ. Xen.

gymnastic exercise, wrestling, Plat., etc.: generally,
exercise, id=Plat.

of the mind,
agony, anguish, ἐν φόβῳ καὶ πολλῇ ἀγωνίᾳ Dem.

like ἀγωνίζομαι,
to contend eagerly, struggle, Dem., etc.
to be distressed, be in an agony, Plat.; περί τινος Arist.; ἐπί τινι Plut.

as Dep.
to contend for a prize, esp. in the public games, Hdt.; πρός τινα Plat.; τινί id=Plat., etc.; περί τινος about a thing, Hdt., etc.: c. acc. cogn., ἀγ. στάδιον id=Hdt.; ἀγῶνα περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς ἀγ. Dem.
to fight, Hdt., Thuc.; περὶ τῶν ἁπάντων ἀγ. id=Thuc.; πρός τινα id=Thuc.: c. acc cogn., ἣν [μάχην] ἀγωνίζεσθε Eur.

to contend for the prize on the stage, both of the poet, Hdt., etc., and of the actor, Dem.: generally
to contend for victory, καλῶς ἠγώνισαι Plat.
of public speaking, Xen.

to contend against, as law-term, Antipho; c. acc. cogn., ἀγ. δίκην, γραφήν
to fight a cause to the last, Dem.; ἀγ. ψευδομαρτυριῶν (sc. γραφήν) id=Dem.; ἀγ. ἀγῶνα Andoc., etc.; but ἀγ. φόνον
to fight against a charge of murder, Eur.

generally,
to struggle, to exert oneself, c. inf., Thuc.; c. acc. cogn., ἃ μὲν ἠγωνίσω Dem.

as Pass.
to be won by a contest, to be brought to issue, mostly in perf., πολλοὶ ἀγῶνες ἀγωνίδαται (ionic for ἠγωνισμένοι εἰσι) Hdt.; τὰ ἠγωνισμένα
the contested points, Eur., etc.; ὁ ἀγωνιζόμενος νόμος the law
under debate, Dem.; fut. mid. in pass. sense, ἀγωνιεῖται τὸ πρᾶγμα it
shall be brought to issue, id=Dem.

of or
belonging to the contest, ἄεθλος ἀγ.
its prize, Pind.; of Hermes, as
president of games, id=Pind.; of Zeus as
decider of the contest, Soph.;—the ἀγώνιοι θεοί, in Aesch., etc., are prob. the gods
who presided over the great games (Zeus, Poseidon, Apollo, Hermes).

ἀγωνίῳ σχολᾷ in Soph. Aj. 195 is prob. an oxymoron, rest
full of conflict, uneasy rest.
contest for a prize, Thuc.

a contest, in pl.
deeds done in battle, brave deeds, feats, Hdt.

in sg., ἀγ. τινός
a feat for him to be proud of, Thuc.; ξυνέσεως ἀγ.
a fine stroke of wit, id=Thuc.; ἀρᾶς ἀγ.
the issue of the curse, Eur.

ἀγ. ποιεῖσθαί τι
to make it an object
to strive for, Hdt.; οὐ μικρὸν τὸ ἀγ. προστάττεις Luc.
that with which one contends, a prize-essay, declamation, ἀγ. ἐς τὸ παραχρῆμα Thuc.
rivalry, Thuc.
one must contend, Xen., etc.

a rival at the games,
competitor, Hdt., etc.:—as adj., ἀγ. ἵπποι
race- horses, Plut.
a debater, opponent, Plat.

c. gen.
one who struggles for a thing, τῆς ἀρετῆς Aeschin.

fit for contest or
debate, Arist.

of persons,
contentious, eager for applause, Plat.:—adv. -κῶς,
contentiously, ἀγ. ἔχειν
to be disposed to fight, Plut.

the office of ἀγωνοθέτης,
direction of games, Plut.
to direct the games, exhibit them, Thuc.; ἀγ. Ὀλύμπια Anth.

c. acc., ἀγ. στάσιν
to stir up sedition, Plut.

generally,
to act as judge, decide, Dem. From

judge of the contests, director of the games, or (later)
an exhibitor of games, Hdt., attic

generally,
a judge, Xen., etc

a number of people brought together, a gathering, assembly, like ἀγορά, ἵζανεν εὐρὺν ἀγῶνα, λῦτο δʼ ἀγών, ἐν ἀγῶνι νεῶν Hom.: esp.
an assembly met to see games, id=Hom., etc.
a place of contest, the arena, id=Hom., etc.; βήτην ἐς μέσσον ἀγῶνα Il.

an assembly of the Greeks
at their great national games, ὁ ἐν Ὀλυμπίῃ ἀγών Hdt.; ὁ Ὀλυμπικὸς ἀγών Ar.

the contest for a prize at the games, ἀγὼν ἱππικός, γυμνικός Hdt., etc.; ἀγὼν τῶν ἀνδρῶν, in which the chorus was composed of men, opp. to τῶν παίδων, Dem., etc.:— hence, ἀγῶνα ἄγειν, καθιστάναι, τιθέναι, προτιθέναι, ποιεῖν, to hold or propose
a contest; ἀγῶν or ἐν ἀγῶνι νικᾶν, to win one or
at one.

generally,
any struggle, trial, or
danger, πολλοὺς ἀγῶνας ἐξιών, of Hercules, Soph.; ἀγὼν προκέαται, c. inf., it is
hard or
dangerous to do a thing, Hdt.:— also, ἀγὼν περὶ τῆς ψυχῆς, περὶ μεγίστων
a struggle for life and death, for one's highest interests, Eur.
a battle, action, Thuc.
an action at law, trial, Plat., etc.

metaph., οὐ λόγων ἔθʼ ἁγών now is not
the time for speaking, etc., Eur.; οὐχ ἕδρας ἀγ. ʼtis no
time for sitting still, id=Eur.

entry.etym: on the augment in the Doric form ἆγον, see Chantraine, MHG, 311.
entry.sense:
to lead or
carry, to convey, bring, with living creatures as the object, φέρω being used of things, δῶκε δʼ ἄγειν ἑτάροισι γυναῖκα, καὶ τρίποδα φέρειν Il. (v. infr. 3); ἄγ. εἰς or πρὸς τόπον; poet. also c. acc. loci, ἄγει Ἀχέροντος ἀκτάν Soph.

intr. of soldiers,
to march, Xen., etc.; so, ἄγωμεν
let us go, NTest.

part. ἄγων is used in sense,
taking, στῆσε δʼ ἄγων, where we should use two Verbs,
took and placed, Hom.
to take with one, ἑταίρους id=Hom.

to carry off as captives or booty, id=Hom., etc.; mostly in phrase ἄγειν καὶ φέρειν
to sweep a country of all its plunder (where φέρειν refers to
things, ἄγειν to
men and cattle); then c. acc. loci, φέρων καὶ ἄγων τὴν Βιθυνίδα
plundering all Bithynia, Xen.; in Pass., ἀγόμεθα, φερόμεθα Eur.

ἄγειν εἰς δίκην or δικαστήριον, ἄγ. ἐπὶ τοὺς δικαστάς
to carry one before a court of justice, Lat. rapere in jus, attic; so, simply ἄγειν, Plat.

to fetch, ἄξεθʼ ὑῶν τὸν ἄριστον Od.: of things,
to bring in, import, οἶνον νῆες ἄγουσι Il.
to draw on, bring on, πῆμα τόδʼ ἤγαγον Οὐρανίωνες id=Il.; Ἰλίῳ φθοράν Aesch.
to bear up, φελλοὶ δʼ ὥς, ἄγουσι δίκτυον id=Aesch.

to lead towards a point,
lead on, τὸν δʼ ἄγε μοῖρα κακὴ θανάτοιο τέλοσδε Il.; also, c. inf., ἄγει θανεῖν
leads to death, Eur.: —ὁδὸς ἄγει the road
leads, εἰς or ἐπὶ τόπον Soph., Plat.

metaph.
to lead, as a general, Il.; ἄγ. στρατιάν, ναῦς, etc., Thuc.; ἄγ. τὴν πολιτείαν
to conduct the government, id=Thuc.
to bring up, train, educate, Plat.

to draw out in length, τεῖχος ἄγειν
to draw a line of wall, Lat. ducere, Thuc.:— Pass., ἦκται ἡ διῶρυξ Hdt.; κόλπου ἀγομένου a bay
being formed, id=Hdt.
to keep in memory, καί μευ κλέος ἦγον Ἀχαιοί Od.

like
agere, to hold, celebrate, ἑορτήν, τὰ Ὀλύμπια Hdt., etc.

also
to hold, keep, observe, σπονδὰς ἄγ. πρός τινας Thuc.; εἰρήνην Plat.: often c. acc., as periphrasis for a Verb, σχολὴν ἄγειν = σχολάζειν, Eur.; ἡσυχίαν ἄγ. = ἡσυχάζειν, Xen.
to keep, maintain, ἐλευθέραν ἦγε τὴν Ἑλλάδα Dem.

of Time,
to pass, ποίας ἡμέρας δοκεῖς μʼ ἄγειν; Soph.

like ἡγέομαι, Lat. ducere, to hold, account, reckon, ἐν τιμῇ ἄγειν, ἐν οὐδεμιῇ μοίρῃ, περὶ πλείστου ἄγειν Hdt.; θεοὺς ἄγειν
to believe in gods, Aesch.; τιμιώτερον ἀγ. τινά Thuc.: —so with Adverbs, δυσφόρως ἄγ.
to think insufferable, Soph.; ἐντίμως ἄγειν Plat.

to weigh so much, ἄγειν μνᾶν, τριακοσίους δαρεικούς
to weigh a mina, 300 darics, Dem., where the acc. is the weight which the thing
weighs or
draws down: cf. ἕλκω.
on ἄγε, ἄγετε, v. sub vocc.

Mid. ἄγομαι,
to carry away for oneself, take with one, χρυσόν τε καὶ ἄργυρον οἴκαδʼ ἄγεσθαι Od.

ἄγεσθαι γυναῖκα, Lat. uxorem ducere, to take to oneself a wife, id=Od.; in full, ἄγ. γυναῖκα ἐς τὰ οἰκία Hdt.; and simply ἄγεσθαι,
to marry, Il., etc.;—also of the father,
to bring home a wife
for his son, Od.

διὰ στόμα ἄγεσθαι μῦθον
to let pass through the mouth, i. e. to utter, Il.

ἄγεσθαί τι ἐς χεῖρας
to take a thing into
one's hands, and so
to undertake, Hdt.

ignorance or
unskilfulness in doing, c. inf., Od.
unknowing, ignorant of a thing, c. gen., Il.; κακῶν ἀδαήμονες Od.

= ἀδαήμων, c. gen. pers., Hdt.; c.gen. rei, id=Hdt.; c. inf.
unknowing how to do, Soph.: absol., Xen.
unknown, Hes.
of which none might eat, Aesch.
without tears, Isocr., Plut.
without tears, i. e.

act. tearless, ἀδ. καὶ ἀπήμων Il.; ἀδακρύτω ἔχεν ὄσσε Od.: —εὐνάζειν ἀδακρύτων βλεφάρων πόθον to lull the desire of her eyes
so that they weep no more, Soph.; cf. ἄδερκτος,

pass.
unwept, unmourned, id=Soph.
costing no tears, τρόπαια Plut.

adamantine, Aesch., etc.: —metaph.
hard as adamant, σιδηροῖς καὶ ἀδαμαντίνοις λόγοις Plat.; οὐκ ἀδ. ἐντί, of a girl, Theocr.:—adv. -νως, Plat.
iron-bound, Aesch.

properly
the untamed, unconquerable:

as Subst.
adamant, i. e. the hardest metal, prob.
steel: metaph. of any thing
unalterable, ἔπος ἐρέω ἀδάμαντι πελάσσας having fixed it
firm as adamant, Orac. ap. Hdt.
the diamond, Theophr.

as adj., metaph.,
the inflexible, of Hades, Theocr.

epith. of Hades,
inflexible, Il.:—later in the proper sense,
untamed, unbroken, ἵππος Xen.

unconquered, Aesch., etc.; of females,
unwedded, Soph.: of beasts, untamed, v. sub πέσημα. [α_δαματω in Theocr.]
without expense, costing nothing, γλυκέα κἀδάπανα (crasis for καὶ ἀδάπανα) Ar.:— adv., ἀδαπάνως τέρψαι φρένα Eur.
undivided, Soph.
without fear, fearless, εἴ περ ἀδειής τʼ ἐστί, of Hector, Il.; κύον ἀδδεές id=Il.

fearless, secure (v. ἀλεής), τὸ ἀδεές,
security, Thuc.; ἀδεὴς θανάτου
without fear of death, Plat.; ἀδεὲς δέος δεδιέναι to fear
where no fear is, id=Plat.
causing no fear, not formidable, πρὸς ἐχθρούς Thuc.

adv. ἀδεῶς,
without fear, confidently, Hdt., etc.
without stint, freely, Thuc.

freedom from fear, ἀδείην διδόναι to grant
an amnesty, indemnity, Hdt.; ἐν ἀδείῃ εἶναι id=Hdt.; τῶν σωμάτων ἄδειαν ποιεῖν Thuc.; ἄδειάν τινι παρασκευάζειν, παρέχειν Dem.; opp. to ἄδειαν λαμβάνειν to receive
indemnity, id=Dem.; ἀδείας τυγχάνειν id=Dem.
fearless, dauntless, Pind., etc.:—adv. -τως, Aesch.
where no fear is, οἰκία Luc.
supperless, Xen., etc.
unbribed, Arist.:—comp. adv. -ότερον Luc.
not tithed, tithe-free, Ar.

fem. of ἀδελφός,
a sister, Trag., etc.
a sister (as a fellow Christian), NTest.

a brother's or
sister's son, a nephew, Hdt.

a brother's or
sister's daughter, a niece, Ar., etc.

murdering a brother or
sister, Hdt. (in ionic form ἀδελφεοκτ-) , Plut.

entry.etym: α copul. , δελφύς; cf. Lat. couterinus
entry.sense:
ἀδελφοί are properly
sons of the same mother:

as Subst., ἀδελφός, ὁ, voc. ἄδελφε (not -φέ), ionic ἀδελφεός, epic -ειός:—
a brother, or generally,
a near kinsman, ἀδελφοί
brother and sister, like Lat. fratres, Eur.; ἀδελφεοὶ ἀπʼ ἀμφοτέρων
brothers by both parents, i. e. not half-brothers, Hdt.
a brother (as a fellow Christian), NTest.

adj., ἀδελφός, ή, όν,
brotherly or
sisterly, Trag., Plat.

like Lat. geminus,
gemellus, of anything
in pairs,
twin, Xen.:—then,
just like, c. gen. or dat., ἀδελφὰ τῶνδε, ἀδελφὰ τούτοισι Soph.
the brotherhood, NTest.
left-handed, awkward, Luc.
unseen, invisible, Anth.

not seeing, ἀδέρκτων ὀμμάτων τητώμενος reft of thine eyes
so that they see not, Soph.; adv. -τως,
without looking, id=Soph.

unfettered, unbound, ἄδ. φυλακή, Lat. libera custodia, our "
parole," Thuc., etc.; δεσμὸς ἄδεσμος bond
that is no bond, of a wreath, Eur.
without master, Plat., etc.
unbound, free, Dem.

a word used by Hom. only in Od. as epith. of ὄλεθρος, πότμος, φῆμις, commonly expl.
not sweet, bitter, cruel (from an old word δευκής
sweet); but more prob. it means
unexpected,
sudden (from δοκ-έω).
untanned, of a raw hide, Od.

entry.etym: only found in two Homeric forms, aor1 opt. and perf. part.
entry.sense:
to be sated, μὴ ξεῖνος δείπνῳ ἀδήσειε lest he
should be sated with the repast,
feel loathing at it; καμάτῳ ἀδηκότες ἠδὲ καὶ ὕπνῳ
sated with toil and sleep.
unassailed, unravaged, Soph.

unbitten, not gnawed or
worm eaten , Hes.; adv. ἀδήκτως, Plut.
to be in the dark about a thing, Soph.
uncertainty, Anth.

not seen or
known, unknown, obscure, Hes., Soph., Plat.

of things, ἄδ. θάνατοι death
by an unknown hand, Soph.; ἄδ. ἔχθρα
secret enmity, Thuc.; ῥεῖ πᾶν ἄδηλον melts all
to nothing, Soph.; ἄδ. τινι
unseen, unobserved by him, Xen.

neut. ἄδηλόν [ἐστι] εἰ . . , ὅτι . . ,
it is uncertain whether . . ,
unknown that . . , Plat., etc.; so, ἄδηλον μή . . , id=Plat.:— absol., ἄδηλον ὄν it being
uncertain, Thuc.; so, ἐν ἀδηλοτέρῳ εἶναι Xen.
ἄδηλος often agrees with the subject (like δίκαιός εἰμι), παῖδες ἄδηλοι ὁποτέρων = ἄδηλόν ἐστιν ὁποτέρων παῖδες εἰσίν Lys., etc.

adv. -λως,
secretly, Thuc., etc.; Sup. -ότατα, id=Thuc.
to be sorely troubled, Plat.; ἀδημονῆσαι τὰς ψυχάς Xen.
trouble, distress, Anth., Plut.

entry.etym: α short, except in first place cited from Il., where it is commonly written ἄδδην.
entry.sense:
adv., Lat. satis, to one's fill, ἔδμεναι ἄδην
to eat their fill, Il.

c. gen., οἵ μιν ἄδην ἐλόωσι πολέμοιο who may drive him
to satiety of war, id=Il.; ἅδην ἔλειξεν αἵματος licked
his fill of blood, Aesch.; καὶ τούτων μὲν ἅδην enough of this, Plat.; c. part., ἄδην εἶχον κτείνοντες Hdt.
without strife, Anth.

without strife or
battle, Il.
unconquerable, ἀνάγκης σθένος Aesch.

entry.etym: αιδης in Hom., attic α?δης; but in Trag. also α_ιδας:— gen. αιδεω as an anapaest in Hom.; gen. αιδα_ο Id=Hom.; gen. α_ιδος before a vowel, Il.
entry.sense:
Hades or
Pluto (cf. Πλούτων), the god of the nether world, son of Kronus and Rhea, brother to Zeus, Ζεὺς καὶ ἐγώ, τρίτατος δʼ Ἄιδης Il.; called Ζεὺς καταχθόνιος id=Il.; εἰν or εἰς Ἀΐδαο (sc. δόμοις, δόμους) in, into the nether world, Hom.; εἰν Ἄϊδος Il.; ἐν Ἅιδου, ἐς Ἅιδου (sc. οἴκῳ, οἶκον) attic:— also Ἄϊδόσδε adv., Il.

as appellative,
Hades,
the world below, εἰσόκεν ἄϊδι κεύθωμαι id=Il.; ἐπὶ τὸν ᾄδην Luc.; εἰς ἀΐδην Anth.; ἐν τῷ ᾄδῃ NTest.

the grave,
death, ᾄδης πόντιος
death by sea, Aesch., etc.

eating one's fill, gluttonous, ἀδ. ἀνήρ, of an athlete, Theocr.; τὴν ἀδ. νόσον this
devouring sore, Soph.
not ravaged, Xen.
not to be passed, ποταμός, νάπος Xen.
not listening to slander, Plut.
intestate, Plut.
undecided, Luc.
unintermitting, incessant, NTest.; adv. -τως, Polyb., NTest.
undissolved, indissoluble, Plat.
unwetted, Simon.

ἀδίαντον, τό, a plant,
maiden-hair, Theocr.
with no way back, of Hades, Eur.
incorruption, uprightness, NTest.
uncorrupted, Plat., etc.:— adv. -ρως, Aeschin.

of judges and witnesses,
incorruptible, Plat., etc.: Sup. adv. -ώτατα, id=Plat.
imperishable, id=Plat.
untaught, ignorant, c. gen., ἀδ. ἐρώτων Anth.
untrained, of a chorus, Dem.

of things,
untaught, Plut., Luc.

act.,
unable to get out, Anth.
unquestioned, Plut.
indescribable, Xen., Dem.
undecided, Luc.

to do wrong, Hdt., etc.; τἀδικεῖν
wrong-doing, Soph.; τὸ μἀδικεῖν
righteous dealing, Aesch.; but, σχήσει τὸ μἀδικεῖν will restrain
wrong-doing, Aesch.:—in legal phrase the particular case of wrong is added in part., Σωκράτης ἀδικεῖ διδάσκων Plat., Xen.:—c. acc. cogn., ἀδικίαν, ἀδίκημα, Plat., or a neut. adj., ἀδικεῖν πολλά, μέγαλα, id=Plat.; οὐδέν, μηδὲν ἀδ., Plat.:—also, ἀδ. περὶ τὰ μυστήρια Dem.

trans. c. acc. pers.
to do one
wrong, to wrong, injure, Hdt., etc.:—c. dupl. acc.
to wrong one
in a thing, Ar., etc.; τὰ μέγιστα ἀδ. τινά Dem.; ἀδ. τινὰ περί τινος Plat.:—Pass.
to be wronged, μὴ δῆτʼ ἀδικηθῶ Soph.; ἀδικεῖσθαι εἴς τι Eur.
to spoil, damage, ἀδ. γῆν Thuc.

a wrong done, a wrong, Lat. injuria, Hdt., etc.:—c. gen.
a wrong done to one, Dem.
that which is got by wrong, ill-gotten goods, Plat.
one must do wrong, Plat.
wrong-doing, injustice, Hdt., etc.

like ἀδίκημα,
a wrong, injury, id=Hdt., Plat.
a wrong, wrong-dealing, Hdt.

ἀδικίου γραφή, an action
against public wrong-doers, Plut.

of persons,
wrong-doing, unrighteous, unjust, Hes., Hdt., etc.; ἀδικώτατος Soph.:— ἄδ. εἴς τι
unjust in a thing, ἔς τινα
towards a person, Hdt.; περί τινα Xen.; c. inf.
so unjust as to . . NTest.

ἄδ. ἵπποι
obstinate, unmanageable, Xen.

of things,
wrongly done, wrong, unjust, ἔργματα Theogn., Hdt., etc.; τὸ δίκαιον καὶ τὸ ἄδ., τὰ δίκαια καὶ ἄδικα right and
wrong, Plat.

adv. -κως, Solon, etc.; τοὺς ἀδ. θνήσκοντας Soph.; εἴτε δικαίως εἴτε ἀδ.

entry.etym: Commonly derived from α privat. , μαζός, from the fable that they got rid of the right breast, that it might not interfere with the use of the bow.

entry.etym: from obsol. ἁμός = τὶς, only in compd. ἀμωσ-γέ-πως
entry.sense: in some way or other, Ar., Plat.
conditional Particle. In attic, it is not joined with pres. or perf. ind., nor with imperat. of any tense. Three uses of ἄν must be distinguished in practice:
in combination with Conjunctions and Relatives.
in Apodosis.
in Iterative sentences.
in combinations with Conjunctions and Relatives:

such words are regularly foll. by the subj., viz. ἐάν (= εἰ ἄν) ἤν, ἄν , ἐπήν; ὃς ἄν
quicunque, πρὶν ἄν, etc.; ἐπειδάν, ὅταν, ὁπόταν: the protasis generally has a fut. in apodosis, εἰ δέ κεν ὣς ἔρξηις, γνώσηι if
perchance thou do thus, thou shalt know, Il.

in epic sometimes with Opt., ὥς κε δοίη ὧι κʼ ἐθέλοι that he
might give her to whomsoever he
might please, Od.: in such cases κε or ἄν does not affect the Verb.
in epic, sometimes with εἰ and Ind., οἵ κέ με τιμήσουσι Il.
in late Greek, ἐάν, etc., take Ind., ἐὰν οἴδαμεν NTest.

combined IN APODOSIS with the Verb, denoting that the assertion is dependent on some condition; ἦλθεν
he came, ἦλθεν ἄν
he would have come; ἔλθοι
may he come, ἔλθοι ἄν
he would come:
with Ind.:

with imperf. and aor., the protasis implies non-fulfilment of a condition, and the apod. expresses what
would be or
would have been the case if the condition
were or
had been fulfilled. The imperf. with ἄν refers to continued action in present or past time, the aor. generally to action in past time; οὐκ ἂν νήσων ἐκράτει, εἰ μὴ ναυτικὸν εἶχεν he
would not
have been master of islands if he had not had a fleet, Thuc.; εἰ ταύτην ἔσχε τὴν γνώμην, οὐδὲν ἂν ἔπραξεν if he had come to this opinion, he
would have accomplished nothing, Dem.:—the protasis is often understood, οὐ γὰρ ἦν ὅ τι ἂν ἐποιεῖτε for there was nothing which you
could have done (i. e.
if you had tried), id=Dem.:—hence the Ind. with ἄν represents a potential mood; ἦλθε τοῦτο τοὔνειδος τάχʼ ἄν this reproach
might perhaps have come, Soph.

in epic, with fut. ind., so as to modify the simple fut.; καί κέ τις ὧδʼ ἐρέει and some one
will perchance speak thus, Il.

with Subj., in epic, much like fut. ind., εἰ δέ κε μὴ δώηισιν, ἐγὼ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι, i. e.
I will take her myself, id=Il.
with Opt.:

after protasis in opt. with εἰ or some relative word, εἴ μοί τι πίθοιο, τό κεν πολὺ κέρδιον εἴη if he should obey me, it
would be much better, id=Il.; sometimes with ind. in protasis, καί νύ κεν ἔνθʼ ἀπόλοιτο, εἰ μὴ νόησε
he would have perished, had she not perceived, id=Dem.:—sometimes the tense in protasis is pres. or fut., and the opt. with ἄν in apodosis= fut., φρούριον εἰ ποιήσονται, βλάπτοιεν ἄν if they shall build a fort, they
might perhaps damage, Thuc.

the protasis is often understood: τὸν δʼ οὔ κε δύʼ ἀνέρε ὀχλίσσειαν two men
could not heave the stone (i. e.
if they should try), Il.:—hence the opt. with ἄν becomes a potential mood, βουλοίμην ἄν
I should like, Lat. velim (but ἐβουλόμην ἄν
I should wish, if it were of any avail,
vellem).

the opt. with ἄν comes to have the force of a mild command or entreaty, χωροῖς ἂν εἴσω you
may go in, Soph.; κλύοις ἂν ἤδη hear me now, id=Soph.

with inf. and part.:—the pres. inf. or part. represents imperf. ind., φησὶν αὐτοὺς ἐλευθέρους ἂν εἶναι, εἰ τοῦτο ἔπραξαν he says they
would (now) be free, if they had done this, Dem.; ἀδυνάτων ἂν ὄντων [ὑμῶν] ἐπιβοηθεῖν when you
would have been unable to assist, Thuc.;—or represents pres. opt., φησὶν αὐτοὺς ἐλευθέρους ἂν εἶναι, εἰ τοῦτο πράξειαν he says they
would (hereafter) be free,
if they should do this, Xen.;—the aor. inf. or part. represents aor. ind. or opt., οὐκ ἂν ἡγεῖσθʼ αὐτὸν κἂν ἐπιδραμεῖν; do you not think he
would even have run thither? Dem.; οὐδʼ ἂν κρατῆσαι αὐτοὺς τῆς γῆς ἡγοῦμαι I think they
would not even be masters of the land, Thuc.; οὔτε ὄντα οὔτε ἂν γενόμενα, i. e.
things which are not and never could happen, id=Thuc.:—so the perf. (or plup.) inf. or partic., πάντα ταῦθʼ ὑπὸ τῶν βαρβάρων ἂν ἑαλωκέναι [φήσειεν ἄν] he would say that all these
would have been destroyed by the barbarians, Dem.

with imperf. and aor. ind. in the ITERATIVE construction, to express
a condition fulfilled whenever an opportunity offered; εἶτα πῦρ ἂν οὐ παρῆν then
there would be no fire at hand, i. e. there never was, Soph.; διηρώτων ἂν αὐτοὺς τί λέγοιεν Plat.
GENERAL REMARKS:
Position of ἄν.

ἄν may be separated from its inf. by such verbs as οἴομαι, δοκέω, so that ἄν has the appearance of belonging to the pres. ind., καὶ νῦν ἡδέως ἄν μοι δοκῶ κοινωνῆσαι I think that I
should, Xen.:—in the peculiar case of οὐκ οἶδʼ ἂν εἰ, ἄν belongs not to οἶδα but to the Verb which follows, οὐκ οἶδʼ ἂν εἰ πείσαιμι = οὐκ οἶδα εἰ πείσαιμι ἄν, Eur.
ἄν never begins a sentence.
Repetition of ἄν:— in apodosis ἄν may be repeated with the same verb, ὥστʼ ἄν, εἰ σθένος λάβοιμι, δηλώσαιμʼ ἄν Soph.

again, and so

to force, compel, mostly c. acc. pers. et inf., ἀν. τινὰ ποιεῖσθαι τι, λέγειν, etc., Hdt., etc.:—so Pass., ἠναγκάζοντο ἀμύνεσθαι id=Hdt.;—without the inf., ἀναγκάζεσθαί τι

to constrain by argument, Plat.: Pass., ἠναγκάσθην

c. acc. rei only,
to carry through by force, Eur.

c. acc. rei et inf.
to prove that a thing

with or
by force:

act.
constraining, applying force, Il.; ἦμαρ ἀν. the day
of constraint, i. e.
slavery, Ib.;so, ἀναγκαία τύχη the lot

necessarily, of necessity, perforce, ἀναγκαίως ἔχει it

interrog. Particle, in accent and sense a stronger form of ἄρα:
in prose, ἆρα almost always stands first in the sentence.
EPIC USAGE:

then, straightway, at once, ὣς φάτο, βῆ δʼ ἄρʼ ὄνειρος Il.:
next in order, οἱ δʼ ἄρʼ Ἀθήνας εἶχον id=Il.

where attention is called to something startling, τὸν τρεῖς μὲν ἐπιρρήσσεσκον τῶν ἄλλων, Ἀχιλεὺς δʼ ἄρʼ ἐπιρρήσεσκε καὶ οἶος three men of the common sort were required to do it, but Achilles,
mark ye did it single-handed, id=Il.

in
explanation of a thing going before, εἰ μὴ ὑπερφίαλον ἔπος ἔκβαλε, φῆ ῥʼ ἀέκητι θεῶν φυγέειν had he not let fall an impious word, —
for he said . . , id=Il.:—so, ἄρα makes relat. Pron. more precise, ἐκ δʼ ἔθορε κλῆρος, ὃν ἄρʼ ἤθελον αὐτοί
just the one, the
very one which . . , id=Il.

ATTIC USAGE, much like οὖν,
then, therefore:— less strongly, μάτην ἄρʼ ἥκομεν
so then we have come in vain, Soph.; εἰκότως ἄρα οὐκ ἐγίγνετο Xen.:—
in questions, to express
the anxiety of the questioner, as τίς ἄρα ῥύσεται; oh!
who is there to save? Aesch.
POSITION: ἄρα never begins a sentence, cf. οὖν, Lat. igitur.

without trembling, without motion, Hom.; ἀτρέμας εὕδειν id=Hom.; ἀτρέμας ἧσο sit
still, Il.; ἀτρέμας ἔχειν to keep
quiet, Hdt.; ἀτρ. ἅπτεσθαί τινος
gently, softly, Eur.; ἀτρ. πορεύεσθαι to go
softly, Xen.

not to tremble, to keep still or
quiet, Hes.; οὐδαμᾶ κω ἠτρεμήσαμεν, of a restless people, Hdt. From
not trembling, unmoved, Plat., Xen. adv. ἀτρεμέως Theogn.
a keeping still, ἀτρεμίαν ἔχειν or ἄγειν Xen.

to keep quiet, Theogn., Hdt.; οὐκ ἀτρ.
to be restless, id=Hdt.
unmoved, immutable, Plut., Luc.

not trembling, unfearing, fearless, Lat. intrepidus, Trag.: c. gen., ἄτρ. μάχας
fearless of fight, Aesch.; so, ἄτρ. ἐν μάχαις Soph.; ἄτρ. εὕδειν
securely, id=Soph.:—also neut. pl. ἄτρεστα as adv., Eur.
unconquered, Aesch.

not rubbed: of places,
not traversed, pathless, Thuc.: of roads,
not worn or
used, Xen.: generally,
fresh, new, Lat. integer, id=Xen.

of hands,
not worn by work, Od.; of corn,
not threshed, Xen.; ἄτρ. ἄκανθαι thorns
on which one cannot tread, or
untraversed thorns, Theocr.
intrepid, dauntless, Il.
inflexibility, Theogn.
unchangeable, eternal, Theocr.
inflexible, unbending, Anth.:—hence Ἄτροπος, ἡ, name of one of the Μοῖραι or Parcae, Hes.; v. Κλωθώ.
to pine away, suffer from atrophy, Plut.
not fed, ill-fed, Xen.
yielding no harvest, unfruitful, of the sea, Hom.; of the air, id=Hom.

c. gen., ἀτρ. κακῶν
not worn out by ills, Aesch.

not worn away, untiring, unwearied, Aesch.:
indefatigable, Plut.

of things,
unabating, Soph., Mosch.; of a road,
wearisome, Theocr.
the unwearied, a name of Pallas, Hom.
entry.etym: Lengthd. form of ἀτρύτη, as Ἀϊδωνεύς of Ἅιδης.

entry.sense: unwounded, Aesch., Soph.
invulnerable, Eur.

a bird, prob. a kind of
partridge; or, as others think, the
godwit or
redshank, Ar.

a bird, prob. a kind of
grouse, attagen Ionicus, Hor.

a salutation used to elders,
father, Hom.

a cry of pain or
grief, Trag., Ar.

a kind of
locust without wings, Hdt.
Ἀττης Ὕης, a form of exorcism, used by the priests of Cybele, Dem.
to side with the Athenians, Thuc., Xen.
a siding with Athens, attachment to her, Thuc.
in the Attic dialect, Dem.
my little Athenian, Ar.

Attic, Athenian, Solon, etc.; ἡ Ἀττική (sc. γῆ),
Attica, Hdt., etc.; cf. Ἀτθίς.

Adv. -κῶς
in Attic style, Dem.
a comic alteration of Ἀττικός, after the form of Λακονικός, Ar.

Pass. :
to be distraught from fear, mazed, bewildered, Hom.; ἀτυζόμενοι πεδίοιο
fleeing bewildered o'er the plain, Il.: also
to be distraught with grief, ἀτυζόμενος Soph., Eur.: c. acc., ὄψιν ἀτυχθείς
amazed at the sight, Il.

in late Ep. we find the Act. ἀτύζω, with 3 sing. aor. 1 opt. ἀτύξαι,
to strike with terror, Theocr.
without burial, Anth.
without a tomb, Luc.
not ruled by tyrants, Thuc.

without pride or
arrogance, modest, Plat.

to be unlucky or
unfortunate, fail, miscarry, Hdt., Thuc., etc.

c. gen.,
to fail of a thing,
fail in getting or
gaining it, τῆς ἀληθείας Xen.; so, c. part., Thuc.

ἀτ. πρός τινα
to fail with another, i. e. to fail in one's request, Xen.:—Pass., τὰ ἀτυχηθέντα
mischances, failures, Dem.
a misfortune, mishap, Oratt.
luckless, unfortunate, Dem., etc.
ill-luck:—a misfortune, miscarriage, mishap, Xen.
again, anew, afresh, once more, Hom., etc.; after numerals, δεύτερον αὖ, τρίτον αὖ, etc., id=Hom.

generally,
again, i. e.
further, moreover, besides, Lat. porro, Od., attic
in turn, on the other hand, following δέ, Il., attic.
the pleon. phrases, πάλιν αὖ, αὖ πάλιν, ἔμπαλιν αὖ, αὖθις αὖ, αὖθις αὖ πάλιν, are only attic, mostly Trag.

αὖ αὖ,
bow wow, of a dog, Ar.
to dry Od., Hdt., Xen.

to dry or
parch up, αὐανῶ βίον
I shall waste life
away, Soph.: Pass., αὐανθείς
withered, Aesch.; so in fut. mid., αὐανοῦμαι
I shall wither away, Soph.

dry, parched, Hes.; of eyes,
dry, sleepless, Anth.
to view in the clearest light, see distinctly, discern, Soph.; so in Mid., Il., Hes.

of the sun,
to beam upon, illumine, τινά Eur.

the light of the sun, sunlight, and in pl.
his rays or
beams, Hom.; ὑπʼ αὐγὰς ἠελίοιο, i.e. still alive, Od.; so, αὐγὰς ἐσιδεῖν, λεύσσειν, βλέπειν Theogn., Aesch., Eur.; but, ὑπʼ αὐγὰς λεύσσειν or ἰδεῖν τι to hold up to
the light and look at, id=Eur.; κλύζειν πρὸς αὐγάς to rise surging towards
the sun, Aesch.:—metaph., βίου δύντος αὐγαί "life's setting
sun, " id=Aesch.:— αὐγή
the dawn, day-break, NTest.

generally,
any bright light, as of fire, Hom.; of lightning, Il.; of the eyes, Soph.; hence αὐγαί, like Lat. lumina, the eyes, Eur.

any gleam on the surface of bright objects,
sheen, αὐγὴ χαλκείη Il.; αὐγὰ πέπλου Eur.
to cry out, speak, Hdt.: an aor1 act. αὔδαξα occurs in Anth.
c. acc. rei,
to utter sounds, speak, Il., Eur.

c. acc. rei,
to speak or
say something, Il., Soph.: so as Dep., id=Soph.:—Pass., ηὐδᾶτο γὰρ ταῦτα so
'twas said, id=Soph.
c. acc. pers.,

to speak to, address, accost, Hom.:
to invoke a god, Eur.

c. acc. et inf.
to tell, bid, order one to do, Soph.; αὐδ. τινα μὴ ποιεῖν
to forbid one to do, Aesch.; αὐδῶ σιωπᾶν Soph.: so as Dep., id=Soph.

to call by name, call so and so, Eur.: Pass., αὐδῶμαι παῖς Ἀχιλλέως Soph.; κάκιστʼ αὐδώμενος most ill
reported of, Aesch.

like λέγειν,
to mean such an one, Eur.

speaking with human voice, Od.; when θεὸς αὐδήεσσα is applied to Calypso and Circe, it means a goddess
who used the speech of mortals, id=Od.
the human voice, speech, opp. to ὀμφή (a divine voice), Il.

the sound or
twang of the bowstring, Od.; of a trumpet, Eur.; of the τέττιξ, Hes.

= φήμη,
a report, account, Soph., Eur.
an oracle, id=Eur.

to draw back or
backwards, Il.;
to draw the bow, id=Il.: absol., in a sacrifice,
to draw the victim's head
back, so as to cut its throat, id=Il.
entry.etym:
It can hardly be a compd. of αὖ ἐρύω, for αὖ is never elsewh. used in the local sense of
back: perh. for ἀνερύω, i. e. ἀνϝερύω.

entry.sense: self-will, wilfulness, stubbornness, contumacy, presumption, Aesch., etc.

self-willed, wilful, dogged, stubborn, contumacious, presumptuous, Hdt., etc.:— metaph. of things,
remorseless, unfeeling, Aesch.:— adv. -δως, Ar.; comp. -έστερον, Plat.

Dep.
to be self-willed, Plat.
an act of self-will, wilfulness, Aesch.
self-willed in speech, Ar.
of the same blood, a brother, sister, kinsman, Soph.; so αὔθαιμος, ον, id=Soph.
self-chosen, self-elected, Xen.

by free choice, of oneself, Eur.:
independent, Thuc.

of things
taken upon oneself, self-incurred, voluntary, Soph., Thuc., etc.
one who calls each thing by its name, Arist.
to have full power over, τινός NTest.

entry.etym: The part -έντης is of uncertain deriv.
entry.sense:
one who does anything
with his own hand, an actual murderer, Hdt., Eur., etc.:—more loosely,
one of a murderer's family, id=Eur.
an absolute master, autocrat, id=Eur.

as adj., αὐθέντης φόνος, αὐθένται θάνατοι murder
by one of the same family, Aesch.

made or
done on the very day, Aeschin.

adv. αὐθημερόν (oxyt.),
on the very day, on the same day, immediately, Aesch., etc.; ionic αὐτημερόν, Hdt.

born on the spot, born in the country, native, Lat. indigena, Hdt.; αὐτ. ποταμοί rivers
that rise in the country, id=Hdt.; ὕδωρ αὐτ.
a natural spring, id=Hdt.:—
genuine, sincere, Eur.

on the spot, here, there, Hom.; αὖθι ἔχειν to keep him
there, as he is, Od.

of Time,
forthwith, straightway, Il.
a lengthd. form of αὖ:

of place
back, back again, Il.; ἂψ αὖτις id=Il.; this sense rare in attic

of Time,
again, afresh, anew, Hom., attic; strengthd., ὕστερον αὖτις, ἔτʼ αὖτις, πάλιν αὖτις Il., etc.; βοᾶν αὖθις to cry
encore! Xen.

of future Time,
again, hereafter, Il., Aesch.

of Sequence,
moreover, in turn, on the other hand, id=Aesch., Soph.
epith. of the Trojans in Il., either

(α copul. , ἰαχή)
loud-shouting, noisy, or,

(from α privat. )
noiseless, silent.
tracing furrows, Anth.

metaph. of
a wife as
the bearer of children, Soph., Eur.

metaph. also,
a furrow in the skin, a gash, wound, Aesch., Eur.

= ὄγμος,
a swathe, Theocr. (Prob. from same Root as ὁλκός, Lat. sulcus, from ἕλκω.)

of or
belonging to the αὐλή or
court, ἐπʼ αὐλείηισι θύρηισι at the door

outer door,
house- door, Od.; so in Hdt. and attic

entry.etym:
prob. from ἄημι (ἄϝημι)
to blow, for the αὐλή was open to the air
entry.sense:
in Hom.
the court-yard, surrounded with out-buildings, and having the altar of Ζεὺς Ἑρκεῖος in the middle, so that it was at once the meeting-place of the family, and the cattle-yard, Il.: it had two doors, viz. the house-door (cf. αὔλειος), and another leading through the αἴθουσα into the πρόδομος, Od.
the wall of the court-yard, Il.

after Hom., the αὐλή was
the court or
quadrangle, round which the house itself was built, having a corridor (περιστύλιον), from which were doors leading into the men's apartments; opposite the house-door (cf. αὔλειος) was the μέσαυλος or μέταυλος (q.v.), leading into the women's part of the house, Hdt., attic

generally,
any court or
hall, Hom., Trag.
flute-playing, Plat.
a flute-player, Lat. tibicen, Theogn., Hdt., etc.
a flute-girl, Lat. tibicina, Ar., Xen., etc.

Αὐλιάδες Νύμφαι Nymphs
protecting cattlefolds, Anth.

a country house, cottage, Hhymn.:
a fold, stable, Eur., Xen.
a chamber, cave, grotto, Soph.

of or
for farm-yards, rustic, Eur.

Dim. of αὐλός,
a small reed, pipe, Theogn.
a place for passing the night in, a tent, roosting-place, Hom., Eur.
a house-mate, Theocr.
a flute-case, Anth.

to make flutes or
pipes, Anth.

sc. τέχνη,
flute-making, Plat.
a flute-maker, Plat.

a flute or rather
clarionet (for it was played by a mouthpiece, γλωσσίς, Aeschin.), Il., etc.; αὐλοὶ ἀνδρήϊοι and γυναικήϊοι, Lat. tibiae dextrae and
sinistrae, bass and treble, Hdt.; sometimes one person played two αὐλοί at once, Theocr.; αὐλὸς Ἐνυαλίου, i. e. a trumpet, Anth.:— ὑπʼ αὐλοῦ to the sound of
the flute, Hdt.; so, πρὸς αὐλόν, ὑπὸ τὸν αὐλόν Xen.

any tube or
pipe, as
the socket of a spear-head,
the groove into which the tongue of a buckle fitted, Hom.;

the master, τίς οὗτος;—Αὐτός, i. e. Socrates, Ar.; similarly in neut. αὐτὸ δείξει
the result will shew, Eur.
of oneself, of one's own accord, Lat. sponte, Hom., Soph.

by oneself, alone, αὐτός περ ἐών although
alone, Il.; αὐτοί ἐσμεν we are
by ourselves, i. e.
among friends, Ar.

in Plat., τὸ δίκαιον αὐτό right

in dat. with Subst.,
together with, ἀνόρουσεν αὐτῆι σὺν φόρμιγγι he sprang up lyre
in hand, Il.; αὐτῆι σὺν πήληκι helmet
and all, id=Il.; and without σύν, αὐτοῖς ἀνδράσι men
and all, Hdt., etc.

added to ordinal Numbers, e. g. πέμπτος αὐτός
himself the fifth, i.e.
himself with four others, Thuc.

in connexion with the person. Pron., ἐγὼ αὐτός, ἐμέθεν αὐτῆς, σὲ αὐτόν, etc., Hom.; in Hdt. and attic it coalesces with oblique cases of Pron., ἐμαυτοῦ, σε-αυτοῦ, ἑ-αυτοῦ:— it is joined with these reflexive Pronouns to add force, αὐτὸς καθʼ αὑτοῦ, αὐτοὶ ὑφʼ αὑτῶν Aesch., etc.
gen. αὐτοῦ is used with the possessive Pron., πατρὸς κλέος ἠδʼ ἐμὸν αὐτοῦ Il.
αὐτὸς ἑαυτοῦ is also used with comp. and Sup. adj. to express something unusual, αὐτὸς ἑωυτοῦ πολλῶι ὑποδεέστερος Hdt.

he, she, it, for the simple Pron. of 3 person,
only in oblique cases, and never at the beginning of a sentence, Hom., attic: cf. ἑαυτοῦ.

with Article ὁ αὐτός, ἡ αὐτή, τὸ αὐτό, and attic contr. αὑτός, αὑτή, ταὐτό and ταὐτόν, gen. ταὐτοῦ, dat. ταὐτῶι, pl. neut. ταὐτά: ionic ὡὐτός, τὠυτό:—
the very one, the same, Lat. idem, Hom., Hdt., attic:—it freq. takes a dat., like ὅμοιος, to denote
sameness, τὠυτὸ ἂν ὑμῖν ἐπρήσσομεν we should fare
the same as you, Hdt.; also, ὁ αὐτὸς καί, cf. Lat. simul ac, id=Hdt.

natural, native, not made, as in αὐτόκτιτος.

just, exactly, as in αὐτόδεκα.

together with, as in αὐτόπρεμνος, αὐτόρριζος.

Β, β, , indecl., second letter of the Gr. alphabet: hence as numeral, βʼ = δύο, δεύτερος, ,β = 2000.
β is the medial labial mute, between tenuis τ and asp. θ. The dialectic variations of β seem to be mostly due to uncertainties of pronunciation:

for γ, as βλήχων γληχών, βλέφαρον doric γλέφαρον, βουνός γουνός· βεμβράς for μεμβράς, βροτός for μορτός
(mortalis).
β is sometimes inserted between μλ, μρ to give a fuller sound, as in ἄμβροτος, μεσημβρία, γαμβρός, μέμβλεται.

entry.etym:
γί-γνομαι is syncopated from γι-γένομαι, the Root being ΓΕΝ; cf. aor. 2 γενέσθαι, γένος, etc.; so Lat. gi-gno for
gi-geno.
entry.sense:
Radical sense,
to come into being, Lat. gigni:

of persons,
to be born, νέον γεγαώς new
born, Od.; γεγονέναι ἔκ τινος Hdt.; more rarely ἀπό τινος id=Hdt.; τινος Eur.:—with Numerals, ἔτεα τρία καὶ δέκα γεγονώς, Lat. natus annos tredecim, Hdt., etc.

of things,
to be produced, Plat., Xen., etc.:—of sums, ὁ γεγονὼς ἀριθμός
the result or
amount, Plat.

of events,
to take place, come to pass, come on, happen, and in past tenses
to be, Hom., etc.:— ὃ μὴ γένοιτο, Lat. quod dii prohibeant, Dem.:—c. dat. et part., γίγνεταί τί μοι βουλομένωι, ἀσμένωι I am glad at
its being so, Thuc., etc.:—of sacrifices, omens, etc.,
to be favourable, id=Thuc., Xen.:—in neut. part., τὸ γενόμενον
the event, the fact, Thuc.; τὰ γενόμενα
the facts, Xen.; τὰ γεγενημένα
former events, the past, id=Xen.; τὸ γενησόμενον
the future, Thuc.:—of Time, ὡς τρίτη ἡμέρη ἐγένετο
arrived, Hdt.

followed by a Predicate,
to come into a certain state,
to become, Lat. fieri, and (in past tenses),
to be so and so, Hom., etc.; πάντα γιγνόμενος
turning every way, Od.; so, παντοῖος γ. Hdt.; τί γένωμαι; what
am I to become? i. e. what is to become of me? Aesch.; οὐκ ἔχοντες ὅ τι γένωνται Thuc.

with Adverbs, κακῶς ἐγένετό μοι
it went ill with me, Hdt.; εὖ, καλῶς, γίγνεται
it goes well, etc., Xen.
followed by oblique cases of Nouns,

c. gen., γ. τῶν δικαστέων
to become one of the jurymen, Hdt., etc.:—
to fall to the share of, belong to, ἡ νίκη γίγνεταί τινος Xen.:—
to be master of, ἑαυτοῦ γ. Soph., etc.; γ. ἐντὸς ἑωϋτοῦ Hdt.:—of things,
to be at, i. e.
to cost, so much, c. gen. pretii, Ar.

with Preps., γ. ἀπὸ, or ἐκ δείπνου
to be done supper, Hdt.; γ. εἰς τόπον
to be at . . , id=Hdt.:—. γ. ἐξ ὀφθαλμῶν τινι
to be out of sight, id=Hdt.; γ. ἐν τόπωι
to be in a place, id=Hdt.; also, γ. ἐν ποιήσει
to be engaged in poetry, id=Hdt., etc.; γ. διʼ ἔχθρας, διʼ ἔριδος γ. τινι
to be at enmity with, Ar., etc.:— γ. ἐπί τινι
to fall into or
be in one's power, Xen.:— γ. μετά τινος
to be on his side, id=Xen.:— γ. παρά τινα
to come to one, Hdt.:— γ. πρὸς τόπωι
to be at or
near . . , Plat.: γ. πρός τινι
to be engaged in . . , Dem.; πρός τι Plat.:— γ. πρὸ ὁδοῦ
to be forward on the way, Il.

entry.etym: γιγνώσκω is redupl. from root ΓΝΩ, cf. γνῶναι, γνωτός, etc.: so Lat. gnosco.
entry.sense:

to know, c. acc., Hom., etc.:—also
to discern, distinguish, ὡς εὖ γιγνώσκηις ἠμὲν θεὸν ἠδὲ καὶ ἄνδρα that

the knees as a suppliant, Il.; so ἑλεῖν, λαβεῖν, γούνων id=Il.; τῶν γουνάτων λαβέσθαι Hdt.; περὶ or ἀμφὶ γούνασί τινος χεῖρας βαλεῖν Od.; ἀμφὶ γόνυ τινὸς πίπτειν Eur.; γούνων λίσσεσθαι to supplicate

on one's

lap (as an offering), id=Il.; metaph., θεῶν ἐν γούνασι κεῖται, i. e. rests on their will and pleasure, Hom.

the knees are in Hom. the seat of strength; hence, γούνατά τινος λύειν to weaken, lame, kill him, Il.: also, metaph., ἐς γόνυ βάλλειν to bring down upon
the knee, i. e. to humble, conquer, Hdt.

entry.etym: The regular sg. is Γοργώ, gen. Γοργοῦς, dat. Γοργοῖ : later, cases were formed as if from a nom. Γοργών, sc. gen. Γοργόνος; dat. Γοργόνι:— in pl., Γοργόνες, acc. -ας are the only forms.
entry.sense:
the Gorgon, i. e.
the grim one (cf. γοργός), Hom.: Hes. speaks of three Gorgons, Euryale, Stheino, Medusa, —the last being
the Gorgon; her snaky head was fixed on the aegis of Athena, and all who looked on it became stone, Eur.

to clasp another's
knees (v. γόνυ I. 2), and so

to implore one
to do a thing, id=Il.; ὑπέρ τινος

entry.etym: Dep. only in pres. and imperf.

entry.sense:
often in Hom., who calls the usual meal δαὶς ἐΐση,
equally divided; Θυέστου δαῖτα παιδείων κρεῶν
the feast of Thyestes
on the flesh of his children, Aesch.; in pl., Od.

of the
meat or
food itself, Eur.
a banqueter, feaster, Aesch., Ar.
from a feast, Od., Theocr.

poet. for δαίς,
a feast, banquet, Il.

to cut up meat,
cut into joints or
to carve, Od.:
to cut up for distribution among the people, Il.
one's portion, δαιτρὸν πίνειν Il.

one that carves meat,
a carver, Od.
the art of carving meat, a helping at table, Od.

one that is entertained, an invited guest, in pl., Hom., Hdt.:—in sg., Plat.; ὁ ξένων δαιτυμών
who makes his meal on strangers, Eur.
a meal, Il.

in Il., mostly, of warriors; in Od., of Ulysses. In the first case (from δάϊς
battle, φρήν)
of warlike mind, warlike;— in the second (from *δάω, φρήν)
wise of mind, prudent. Others take *δάω as the Root in all cases, and translate
skilful, proved.

entry.etym: The Root is ΔΑϜ, which appears in the perf. pass. part. δεδαυμένος, Semon.
the perfect and pluperfect forms are commonly used with the present and imperfect meanings.
entry.sense:
to light up, make to burn, kindle, Lat. accendo, Il., Aesch.:—Pass.
to blaze, burn fiercely, Il.; πυρὶ ὄσσε δεδήει
blazed with fire, Od.; metaph., πόλεμος, μάχη δέδηε war
blazes forth, Il.; ὄσσα δεδήει the report
spread like wild-fire, Lat. flagrat rumor, id=Il.
to burn, burn up, Lat. uro:— Pass., δαισθείς Eur.

to divide; for the Act., δαΐζω is used:— Pass., δαίεται ἦτορ Od.; epic 3rd pl. perf., διχθὰ δεδαίαται
are divided in two, id=Od.:—Mid.
to distribute, κρέα id=Od.—The aor1 ἔδαισα, ἐδαισάμην belong to δαίνυμι; fut. δάσομαι, aor1 ἐδασάμην to δατέομαι.
heart-eating, heart-vexing, Soph.

Dep. : metaph.
to be afflicted, mournful, imperat. δακνάζου Aesch.

to bite, of dogs, Il.; στόμιον δ.
to champ the bit, Aesch.; χεῖλος ὀδοῦσι δακών, as a mark of determination, Tyrtae.; δ. ἑαυτόν
to bite one's lips for fear of laughing, Ar.

metaph. of pungent smoke and dust,
to sting or
prick the eyes, Ar.

of the mind,
to bite or
sting, δάκε φρένας μῦθος Il.; ἔδακε ἡ λύπη Hdt.; so in Trag.: —Pass., of love, δηχθεῖσα Eur.; καρδίαν δέδηγμαι
I was stung, vexed at heart, Ar.
an animal of which the bite is dangerous, a noxious beast, Aesch.; δάκη θηρῶν ravenous beasts, Eur.
that which is wept for, a subject for tears, Orac. ap. Hdt.
that which is wept, a tear, Aesch., Eur.

of persons,
tearful, much-weeping, Hom.; δακρυόεν γελάσαι, as adv., to smile
through tears, Il.

of things,
tearful, causing tears, πόλεμος, μάχη id=Il.
a tear, Hom., Hdt., attic, etc.
anything like tears, gum, Hdt.
= δάκρυμα Ι, Anth.
to swim with tears, of a drunkard, Od.
a tear, Lat. lacruma, Hom., Trag.

like δάκρυον, any
drop, δ. πεύκινον Eur.

to melt into tears, shed tears, Soph.; ἐπί τινι at a thing, Eur.: of the eyes,
to run with tears, id=Eur.
flowing with tears, Eur.
dropping tears, Aesch.
wept over, tearful, Aesch., Anth.
delighting in tears, Anth.

shedding tears, Hom., Aesch.; τινός
for a person, Od.
tearful, lamentable, Luc.

intr.
to weep, shed tears, Hom., etc.; c. acc. cogn., δ. γόους to lament
with tears, Soph.: c. gen. causae,
to weep for a thing, Eur.:—also, δ. βλέφαρα
to flood them
with tears, id=Eur.:—so perf. pass.
to be tearful, be all in tears, Il.
of trees (cf. δάκρυον), Luc.

c. acc.
to weep for, lament, Aesch., Soph., etc.:—Pass.
to be wept for, Aesch., Eur.
a finger-sheath, Xen.
set in a ring, Anth.
the art of cutting gems (for rings), Plat.
engraver of gems, Critias.
a ring, seal-ring, Hdt., Ar.
to point at with the finger, Dem.
pointed at with the finger, Lat. digito monstratus, Aesch.
wearying the fingers by keeping them bent, Anth.

a finger, Lat. digitus, ἐπὶ δακτύλων συμβάλλεσθαι to reckon on
the fingers, Hdt.; ὁ μέγας δ.
the thumb, id=Hdt.

οἱ δ. τῶν ποδῶν
the toes, Xen.; and δάκτυλος alone, like Lat. digitus, a toe, Ar.

the shortest Greek measure of length,
a finger's breadth, = about 7/10 of an inch, Hdt.

a metrical foot,
dactyl, ¯ ˘ ˘, Plat.
worn by fingers, Anth.
a fire-brand, piece of blazing wood, Hom., Aesch.
a thunderbolt, Il.
a burnt-out torch: metaph. of an old man, Anth.
to overpower:

of animals,
to tame, break in, to bring under the yoke: Mid.
to do so for oneself, Hom., Xen.

of maidens,
to make subject to a husband, Il.: Pass.
to be forced or
seduced, Hom.

to subdue or
conquer, id=Hom.: Pass.
to be subject to another, id=Hom.: (hence δμώς, δμωή).
to strike dead, kill, Od.

of wine and the like,
to overcome, overpower, Hom.: Pass.
to be overcome, δεδμημένοι ὕπνωι Il.; οἱ δμαθέντες
the dead, Eur.
browsed by heifers, Anth.
a young steer, Anth.
beef-eating, Anth.

poet. form of δαμάζω,
to subdue, break in: Mid., Eur.
a heifer, Lat. juvenca, Aesch.
a girl, Anth.
a wife, spouse, Il., Trag.
taming mortals, man-slaying, Simon.
one who tames, Anth.
Il.:—Mid., Hom.:—Pass., ὑφʼ Ἕκτορι δάμνατο Il.

= τὰ δημοσίαι ἀιδόμενα,
songs sung in public, Ar.

the sons or
descendants of Danaus, Eur.
daughters of Danaus.

the Danaans, subjects of Δάναος, king of Argos; in Il., for
the Greeks generally.
to put out money at usury, to lend, Plat., etc.

Mid.
to have lent to one, to borrow, Ar.; ἐπὶ μεγάλοις τόκοις at high interest, Dem.

Pass., of the money,
to be lent out, Ar., Xen.
a loan, Dem.
a loan, δ. ποιεῖσθαι = δανείζεσθαι (in mid. sense), Thuc.
money-lending, Plat., etc.: metaph., αἵματος δανεισμός Eur.
a money-lender, Plut., NTest.

of or
for money-lending, Plut.
money lent, a loan, debt, Anth.
burnt, dry, parched, Od.;Sup., δανότατος, Ar.
a firebrand, torch, Hom.

entry.etym: some pass. tenses are also used in depon. sense, pres., imperf., aor1
entry.sense:
to spend, Thuc., etc.; δαπ. εἴς τι
to spend upon a thing, id=Thuc., Xen.; so also as Dep.
to spend, Hdt.; ὅσα δεδαπάνησθε εἰς τὸν πόλεμον Dem.
to expend, consume, use up, Arist.:—metaph. of persons, ὑπὸ νόσου δαπανᾶσθαι Plut.

Causal, τὴν πόλιν δαπανᾶν
to put it
to expense, Thuc.

money spent, Arist.: in pl.
costs, expenses, Xen.

outgoing, cost, expense, expenditure, Hes.; χρημάτων Thuc.; δ. κούφη
the cost is little, Eur.:—also in pl., Thuc.

money spent, ἵππων
on horses, Pind.; δαπάνην παρέχειν
money for spending, Hdt.
extravagance, Aeschin.

of men,
lavish, extravagant, Plat., Xen.

of things,
expensive, Dem., Arist.:—adv. -ρῶς, Xen.

explained by the Scholl. as Dor. for γῆ, in the phrases δᾶ φεῦ, φεῦ δᾶ Aesch., Eur.; οὐ δᾶν no
by earth, Theocr. But it is prob. that δᾶ or Δᾶ is a doric voc. of Δάν = Ζάν (i. e. Ζήν = Ζεύς), and Δᾶν acc. = Ζῆν (i. e. Ζῆνα).
intensive Prefix, = ζα-, as in δά-σκιος, δα-φοινός.

entry.etym: prob. for ζάπεδον, i. e. διάπεδον.
entry.sense:
any level surface: the floor of a chamber, Il., Hdt., Xen.; also, γῆς δάπεδον Ar.; and absol.
the ground, Od.: pl.
plains, Pind., Eur.
a carpet, rug, Ar., Xen.

to devour, as wild beasts, Il.; of fire, id=Il.; of a spear,
to rend, id=Il.: metaph., δάπτει τὸ μὴ ʼνδικον injustice
gnaws the heart, Soph.; δάπτομαι κέαρ Aesch.

a son or
descendant of Dardanus, Il.
Trojan, Il.
a Trojan woman, Il.

Dardanus, son of Zeus, founder of Troy, Il.:—as adj., Δάρδανος ἀνήρ
a Trojan, id=Il.

Il.: κτήματα δαρδάπτουσιν
they devour one's patrimony, Od.

Δα_ρεικὸς στατήρ or Δαρεικός, alone, a Persian gold coin,
a Daric, Hdt., etc. These are said to have been first coined by Darius Hystaspes.
born from Darius, Aesch.

Darius, name of several kings of Persia; being a Greek form of Persian
dara, a king.
to sleep, Od.
thick-shaded, bushy, Od., Eur.; of a beard, Aesch., Soph.
a distributing, Xen.

to collect as tribute, τι παρά τινος Dem.:—c. acc. pers.
exact tribute from him, Isocr.
collection of tribute, Plut.
a tax-gatherer, Strab.
a division, distribution, sharing of spoil, Il., Hhymn.

in attic
an impost, tribute, ἀοιδοῦ δ.
tribute paid to her, Soph.; δασμὸν τίνειν id=Soph.; δασμὸν φέρειν, ἀποφέρειν, ἀποδιδόναι Xen.

to be subject to tribute, Aesch.: —Pass., δασμοφορεῖταί τινι
tribute is paid one, Xen.
paying tribute, tributary, Hdt., Xen.

entry.etym: Perh. from δα, πλήσσω, ς being inserted.
entry.sense: horrid, frightful, Ἐρινύς Od.; of Hecate, Theocr.
thick-haired, hairy, Anth.
bushy-tailed, ἀλώπηξ Theocr.
shaggy-legged, of Pan, Anth.
thick-fleeced, woolly, Od., Eur.

rough-foot, i. e.
a hare, Arist.; λαγωὸς ὁ δ. Babr.
opp. to ψιλός in all senses:

thick with hair, hairy, shaggy, rough, Od.; of young hares,
downy, Hdt.

thick with leaves, Od.; θρίδαξ δασέα a lettuce
with all the leaves on, Hdt.:—of places,
thick with bushes or
wood, id=Od.; διὰ τῶν δασέων through
the copses, Ar.; δ. ὕληι
thick with copse-wood, Hdt., etc.; rarely c. gen., δασὺς δένδρων Xen.:— τὸ δασύ
bushy country, id=Xen.
shaggy-breasted, Hes.
shaggy-haired, Anth.

to divide among themselves, τὰ μὲν εὖ δάσσαντο μετὰ σφισίν Il.; ἄνδιχα πάντα δάσασθαι Hom.; μένος Ἄρηος δατέονται
they share, i. e.
are alike filled with, the spirit of Ares, Il.; of persons at a banquet, κρέα δατεῦντο Od.; διδόναι τινα κυσὶ δάσασθαι
to tear in pieces, Il.

[ἡμίονοι] χθόνα ποσσὶ δατεῦντο
measured the ground with their feet, Lat. carpebant viam pedibus, id=Il.
to cut in two, id=Il.

simply,
to divide, to divide or
give to others, Hdt.:—perf. in pass. sense,
to be divided, Il., Hdt., Eur.
dividing, distributing, Aesch.
a distributer, Aesch.

sc. Δαυλία χώρα
Phocis, Soph.

a woman of Daulis, epith. of Philomela, who was changed into
the nightingale, Thuc.
a Daulian, Hdt.
Daulis, a city of Phocis, Hom., etc.

the laurel, or rather
the bay-tree, Lat. laurus, Od., Hes., etc.; sacred to Apollo, who delivered his oracles ἐκ δάφνης, Hhymn.
to bear a laurel crown, Plut.

laurel-bearing, δ. κλῶνες
laurel branches
borne in worship of Apollo, Eur.
belonging to a laurel, Anth.
delighting in laurel, Anth.
laurel-crowned, Anth.
like laurel: laurelled, Eur.

of savage animals,
blood-red, tawny, δαφοινὸν δέρμα λέοντος Il.; δράκων ἐπὶ νῶτα δαφοινός id=Il.: the form δαφοινεός bears the same sense, εἷμα δαφοινεὸν αἵματι
red with blood, id=Il.; δαφοινὸς ἀετός Aesch., etc.

metaph.
savage, cruel, Hhymn., Aesch.

abundant, plentiful, Hdt.:— adv. -έως,
in abundance, Theocr.

of persons,
liberal, profuse, Plut.:—Sup. adv., δαψιλέστατα ζῆν Xen.

an old Root, δα
to learn, Lat. disco, which becomes Causal,
to teach, Lat. doceo, in redupl. aor2 δέδαε and in διδάσκω:

to learn, and in perf.,
to know; c. gen. pers.
to learn from one, Od.; c. gen. rei,
to hear tidings of a thing, Il. From δέδαα again is formed a pres. mid. inf. δεδάασθαι,
to search out, c. acc., Od.—The pres. in this sense is διδάσκομαι.

Causal, in redupl. aor. 2 δέδαον, c. dupl. acc.
to teach a person a thing, Od.; c. inf.
to teach one to do a thing, id=Od.—The pres. in this sense is διδάσκω.

a word of doubtful origin, expl. by ἐδόκει, ἀεικέλιος δέατʼ εἶναι
he seemed, methought he was, a pitiful fellow, Od.:
to greet, Od.

irreg. partic. of δέχομαι (Ionic δέχομαι), in act. sense,
waiting, lying in wait, Il., Hes.;—not to be confounded with attic δεδόκημαι from δοκέω.
resolved form of δῆλος, Il.
an entreaty, Ar.
an entreating, asking: a prayer, entreaty, Dem., NTest.
suppliant, Plut.

a sample, pattern, proof, specimen, Lat. documentum, Eur., Ar., etc.; δείγματος ἕνεκα by way
of sample, Dem.

a place in the Peiraeeus, where merchants set out their wares for sale,
a bazaar, Xen., Dem.
to make a show of, NTest.
fearful, cowardly, Il.

entry.etym: Dep., only in pres. and imperf.
entry.sense:
to meet with outstretched hand, to greet, welcome, δεξιτερῆι δειδίσκετο χειρί Od.; δέπαϊ δειδίσκετο
pledged him in a cup, id=Od.; also, δεδισκόμενος id=Od.

= δείκνυμι 1,
to show, Hhymn.

Dep.:—Causal of δείδω,
to frighten, alarm, μὴ δειδίσσεο λαὸν Ἀχαιῶν Il.; Ἕκτορα ἀπὸ νεκροῦ δειδίξασθαι
to scare him
from the corpse, id=Il.; οὔ σε ἔοικε δειδίσσεσθαι it beseems not
to attempt to frighten thee, id=Il.:—c. inf., φευγέμεν δειδίσσετο Theocr.:—in attic form, Plat., Dem.

entry.etym: pres. δείδω only in first pers., δέδοικα or δέδια being always used as pres. in attic.
entry.sense:
to fear, absol., Hom., etc.; foll. by a prep., δ. περί τινι
to be alarmed, anxious about . . , Il., attic; ἀμφί τινι, περί τινος, ὑπέρ τινος id=Il.:—followed by a relat. clause with μή . . , Lat. vereor ne . . , I fear it is . . , followed by subj.; rarely by ind., δείδω μὴ νημερτέα εἶπεν Od.; δ. μὴ οὐ . . , Lat. vereor ut . . , I fear it is not . . , foll. by subj., Hdt., etc.

c. inf.
to fear to do, Il., Thuc.

c. acc.
to fear, dread, Hom., etc.

τὸ δεδιός,
one's fearing, = δέος, Thuc.
to wait till evening, σὺ δʼ ἔρχεο δειελιήσας Od.
at evening, Theocr.

of or
belonging to evening, δείελον ἦμαρ
eventide, Od., Theocr.

as Subst. (sub. χρόνος),
late evening, εἰσόκεν ἔλθηι δείελος Il.
to point out, shew, in ionic imperf. δεικανάασκεν Theocr.

Hom. uses it only in Mid. = δειδίσκομαι,
to salute, greet, δεικανόωντʼ ἐπέεσσιν Od.; δεικανόωντο δέπασσι
pledged him, Il.
Lacon. for ὑποκριτής, Lat. mimus, a burlesque actor, Plut.
a representation, exhibition, Hdt.

to bring to light, display, exhibit, Od., etc.:—Mid.
to set before one, Il.

to shew, point out, id=Il., Soph.:—absol., αὐτὸ δείξει experiment
will shew, Plat.; so, δείξει alone, Ar.

to point out by words,
to tell, explain, teach, Lat. indicare, ὁδόν Od., etc.:—
to shew, prove, with part., ἔδειξαν ἕτοιμοι ὄντες
shewed that they were ready, Thuc.

of accusers,
to inform against, τινά Ar.

to offer, proffer, τὰ πιστά Aesch.:
to cause, πήματα id=Aesch.

in Mid., like δειδίσκομαι, δεξιόομαι,
to welcome, greet, τὼ καὶ δεικνύμενος προσέφη Hom.: —so also in perf. and plup. pass., δείδεκτʼ Ἀχιλῆα
he pledged him,
drank to him, Il.; τοὺς μὲν κυπέλλοις δειδέχατο id=Il.; δειδέχαται μύθοισι Od.
to be shown, Xen.

δεικτέον μοι
it is my
duty to show, Dem.

to be a coward or
cowardly, Arist.

lengthd. form of δειλός,
wretched, sorry, paltry, mostly of persons, Trag.; also, δ. χάρις a
sorry kindness, Aesch.; δ. σποδός
paltry dust, Soph., etc. [Penult. is often made short in attic Poets.]

a coward: commonly with a coaxing sense,
poor fellow! Ar.
very pitiable, Ar.

afternoon, ἔσσεται ἢ ἠὼς ἢ δείλη ἢ μέσον ἦμαρ Il.; divided into
early and
late (πρωΐα and ὀψία), περὶ δείλην πρωΐην, or δείλης ὀψίης Hdt.; τῆς δείλης
in the course of the afternoon, Xen.
the late afternoon, evening, id=Xen.

cowardice, Hdt., Soph.; δειλίην ὀφλεῖν to be charged with
cowardice, Hdt.
fright, faintheartedness, Plut.
to be afraid.

Dep.
to verge towards afternoon, δείλετό τʼ ἠέλιος Od.

of persons,
cowardly, craven, Il.; hence,
vile, worthless, id=Il.:— δειλός τινος
afraid of . . , Anth.

miserable, luckless, wretched, Hom.; with a compassionate sense, like Lat. miser, δειλοὶ βροτοί
poor mortals! ἆ δειλέ
poor wretch! ἆ δειλοί
poor wretches! id=Hom.

of things,
miserable, wretched, Hes., Soph.
to be afraid, in a fright, Hhymn., Hdt., etc.

c. acc.
to fear a thing, id=Hdt., Aesch.
timid, Mosch.
horrible, fearful, Batr., Theogn.
fear, affright, Il., Hdt., attic

an object of fear, a terror, horror, ὦ πῦρ σὺ καὶ πᾶν δ. Soph.: esp. in pl., δειμάτων ἄχη
fearful plagues or monsters, Aesch.; δείματα θηρῶν Eur.
frightened, scared, Anth.

to frighten, Hdt., Ar.:— Pass.
to be frightened, Aesch., Eur.
fear, terror:— personified Δεῖμος, Il.
contr. for δέον neut. part., v. δεῖ 111.
such an one, a certain one, whom one cannot or will not name, ὁ δεῖνα Ar., etc.; ὁ δεῖνα τοῦ δεῖνος τὸν δεῖνα εἰσαγγέλλει Dem.
δεῖνα in Com. as an interjection, Lat. malum! plague on't! Ar.
a knave, Mosch.

Dep.
to complain loudly, Hdt.
to complain loudly of sufferings, Dem.
terrible of foot, Ἀρὰ δ. (as if she was a hound upon the track), Soph.

entry.etym: from δέος, properly δεεινός, cf. ἐλεεινός, ἐλεινός, from ἔλεος
entry.sense:
fearful, terrible, dread, dire, Hom., etc.; δεινὸν ἀϋτεῖν, βροντᾶν to shout, thunder
terribly, Il.; δεινὸν δέρκεσθαι, παπταίνειν, ἰδεῖν to look
terrible, Hom.; but, δεινὸς ἰδέσθαι
fearful to behold, Od.; δεινὸς μὲν ὁρᾶν, δεινὸς δὲ κλύειν Soph.:— τὸ δεινόν
danger, suffering, awe, terror, Hdt., Aesch., etc.; so, τὰ δεινά Soph., etc.:— οὐδὲν δεινοί, μὴ ἀποστέωσιν no
fear of their revolting, Hdt.:— δεινὸν ποιεῖσθαι
to take ill, complain of, be indignant at a thing, Lat. aegre ferre, id=Hdt., etc.; δεινὰ παθεῖν to suffer
dreadful, illegal, arbitrary treatment, attic; so in adv., δεινῶς φέρειν Hdt.; δ. ἔχειν to be
in straits, Xen.

with a notion of Force or Power,
mighty, powerful, δεινὸν σάκος
the mighty shield, Il.

simply,
wondrous, marvellous, strange, τὸ συγγενές τοι δεινόν kin has a
strange power, Aesch.; δ. ἵμερος, ἔρως, δέος Hdt.; δεινὸν ἂν εἴη, εἰ . . , it were
strange that . . , Eur.:—adv. -νῶς,
marvellously, exceedingly, δ. μέλας, ἄνυδρος Hdt.

the sense of
powerful, wondrous passed into that of
able, clever, skilful, id=Hdt., attic; esp. of
practical ability, opp. to σοφός, Plat.: c. inf., δεινὸς εὑρεῖν
clever at inventing, Aesch.; δεινὸς λέγειν Soph.; δεινὸς πράγμασι χρῆσθαι Dem.: also c. acc., δεινὸς τὴν τέχνην Plat.; δ. περί τι or τινος id=Plat.

terribleness, Thuc.:
harshness, sternness, severity, νόμων id=Thuc.
natural ability, cleverness, shrewdness, Dem.; esp. in an orator, Thuc., Dem.
to make terrible: to exaggerate, Thuc.
exaggeration, Plat.
fierce-eyed, of the Erinyes, Soph.

to make a meal, Hom.: in attic
to take the chief meal, to dine, δ. τὸ ἄριστον
to make breakfast serve as
dinner, Xen.

c. acc., δ. ἄρτον
to make a meal on bread, Hes.; also, δ. ἀπό τινος Ar.
meal-time, Od.
a dining-room, Plut.
to entertain at dinner, Od., Hdt.
fishing for invitations to dinner, parasitic, Hes.

in Hom.
the principal meal of the day, —sometimes
the noonday meal, sometimes = ἄριστον,
the morning meal, sometimes = δόρπον,
the evening meal. In old attic
the midday or
afternoon meal, dinner or
supper:— ἀπὸ δείπνου straightway after
the meal, Il.; καλεῖν ἐπὶ δεῖπνον; δ. παραθεῖναι, etc.

generally,
fodder, provender, Il., Aesch.

to give a dinner:— Mid.
to dine, Thuc., Xen.
carrying meat-offerings, Plut.

c. acc. pers. et inf., δεῖ τινὰ ποιῆσαι
it is binding on one to do a thing,
one must, one ought, Lat. oportet, Hom., etc.:—rarely, δεῖ σε ὅπως δείξεις = δεῖ σε δεῖξαι, Soph.: —rarely also c. dat. pers. et inf.,
there is need for one to do, δεῖ τινὶ ποιήσαι Eur., Xen.
c. acc. rei et inf., δεῖ τι γενέσθαι Thuc., etc.:—for the phrase οἴομαι δεῖν, v. οἴομαι:— when used absol., an inf. may be supplied, μὴ πεῖθʼ ἃ μὴ δεῖ (sc. πείθειν) Soph., etc.

(from δέω2,
to want), c. gen. rei,
there is need of, there is wanting, Lat. opus est re, οὐδὲν δεῖ τινός Hdt., attic:—phrases, πολλοῦ δεῖ
there wants much, far from it; ὀλίγου δεῖ
there wants little, all but:— in answers, πολλοῦ γε δεῖ, πολλοῦ γε καὶ δεῖ far from it, Ar., Dem.; πλεῦνος δεῖ
it is still further from it, Hdt:— ὀλίγου δεῖν absol., in same sense, Plat.; μικροῦ δεῖν Dem.
with a dat. pers. added, δεῖ μοί τινος, Lat. opus est mihi re, Aesch., Thuc., etc.
with acc. pers. added, δεῖ σε προμηθέως Aesch.

neut. part. δέον, contr. δεῖν, absol., like ἐξόν, παρόν

need, Hdt.

indecl., fourth letter of the Gr. alph.: as numeral, δ' = τέσσαρες and τέταρτος, but ,δ = 4000.
δ is the medial dental mute, between the tenuis τ and the aspirate θ.
changes of δ in the dialects:
aeolic into β, as σάμβαλον for σάνδαλον:— reversely, ὀβελός becomes ὀδελός in doric
aeolic or doric into ζ, or ζ into δ and σδ, v. ζῆτα II. 2
into θ, as ψεῦδος ψύθος.

into λ, as δαήρ, Lat. levir, δάκρυ
lacryma, δασύς λάσιος.
into ς, as ὀδμή ὀσμή, ἴδμεν ἴσμεν.
sometimes δ is inserted to give a fuller sound, (ἀνήρ) ἀνέρος ἀνδρός.
δ is sometimes lost, cf. διωγμός, δίωξις with ἰωκή.

it sometimes represents
j. (y), as in ἤδη or δή, Lat. jam.

anything shaped like a Δ, a name for

Pass.
to grow up to pighood, Ar.

the dolphin, Hom., etc.

shaped like a dolphin, hung at the yard-arm, and suddenly let down on the decks of the enemy's ships, Ar.:—hence, κεραῖαι δελφινοφόροι beams

king of Delphi, Aesch.
the womb, Arist.

the frame of man,
the body, Hom.; rarely of other animals, Od.; properly

in Trag. as a periphrasis, like κάρα, κτανεῖν μητρῷον δ. Aesch.; Ἡράκλειον δ. Eur.; Δαματρὸς ἀκτᾶς δ., i. e. bread, id=Eur.

as adv., δέμας πυρὸς αἰθομένοιο
in form or

mostly in pl. δέμνια,
the bedstead or

generally,
a bed, bedding, Od., etc.

keeping one to one's bed, μοῖρα δ.

he built him houses, Od.:—generally,
to construct, δ. ἀλωήν Hhymn.; δ. ὁδόν, ἁμαξιτόν, Lat. munire viam, Hdt.

a tree, Ar.; δένδρα
fruit-trees (opp. to ὕλη

your right as you sail in, id=Hdt.; used in welcoming, δεξιὰν διδόναι to salute by offering
the right hand, Ar.

the right hand given as a
pledge or
assurance, δεξιαὶ ἧις ἐπέπιθμεν Il.; δεξιὰς δόντες καὶ λαβόντες having exchanged
assurances, made a treaty, Xen.; δεξιὰς παρὰ βασιλέως φέρειν μή . . to bring
pledges that he would not . . , id=Xen.—Though δεξιά is manifestly fem. of δεξιός, it is always used as a Subst. without χείρ; but δ. χείρ occurs in Soph., Eur., Ar.

rich in sacrifices, Eur.

a spearman: in pl.
guards, NTest.: others δεξιοβόλοι

on the right hand or
side, Lat. dexter, opp. to ἀριστερός, Hom., etc.; τὸ δ. (sc. κέρας)

fortunate, boding good, of the flight of birds, δεξιὸς ὄρνις, = αἴσιος, Hom. —This sense came from the Greek augurs looking to the North, so that
lucky omens, which came from the East, were
on the right, while the
unlucky ones from the West were
on the left.

metaph.
dexterous, ready, opp. to σκαιός
(sinister, French
gauche); and of the mind,
sharp, shrewd, clever, Ar., Thuc., etc.:—adv., δεξιῶς; Sup. δεξιώτατα, Ar.
dexterity, cleverness, Hdt., Ar.; opp. to ἀμαθία, Thuc.
receiving fire, Eur.

right, the right, Hom.: δεξιτερή, like δεξιά (sub. χείρ),
the right hand, Il.; epic dat. δεξιτερῆιφι id=Il.

a greeting, canvassing, Lat. ambitus, Plut.

entry.etym: neut. part. of the impers. δεῖ, made into a Noun

that which is binding, needful, right, proper, Soph., Xen.; τὰ δέοντα
things needful or
proper, advantages or
duties, Thuc., etc.; ἐν δέοντι (sc. καιρῶι),

for a needful purpose, id=Hdt.; hence (at Athens) the phrase for
secret service, εἰς τὸ δέον ἀπώλεσα Ar.

fear, alarm, affright, Hom., etc.; τεθνάναι τῶι δέει τινά
to be dead afraid of a person, Dem.
awe, reverence, Aesch.

reason for fear, Il.:
a means of inspiring fear, Thuc.
a beaker, goblet, chalice, Hom.
enclitic Particle, joined,

to names of Places in the acc., to denote
motion towards that place, οἶκόνδε (attic οἴκαδε) home-
wards, ἅλαδε sea-
wards, Οὐλυμπόνδε
to Olympus, θύραζε (for θύρασδε)
to the door, Hom.; sometimes repeated with the possess. Pron., ὅνδε δόμονδε; and sometimes even after εἰς, as εἰς ἅλαδε Od.; in Ἀϊδόσδε it follows the gen., = εἰς Ἅιδου (sc. οἶκον). In attic joined to the names of cities, Ἐλευσῖνάδε, Ἀθήναζε, Θήβαζε (for Ἀθήνασδε, Θήβασδε).

sometimes it denotes
purpose only, μή τι φόβονδʼ ἀγόρευε speak not aught
tending to fear, Il.
-δε is also used to strengthen certain Pronouns, ὅδε, τοιόσδε, etc.

but: conjunctive Particle, with
adversative force: it commonly answers to μέν, and may often be rendered by
while, whereas, on the other hand, v. μέν:— but μέν is often omitted, δέ being used merely to pass on from one thing to another; ὣς Ἀχιλεὺς θάμβησεν, θάμβησαν δὲ καὶ ἄλλοι Il.; etc.; κινεῖ κραδίην κινεῖ δὲ χόλον Eur.
δέ is often redundant,

to introduce the apodosis, where it may be rendered by
then, yet, εἰ δέ κε μὴ δώωσιν, ἐγὼ δέ κεν αὐτὸς ἕλωμαι if they will not give it,
then I will take it, Il.; so
at in Lat.,
si tu oblitus es, at Dii meminerint Catull.

to resume after interruption caused by a parenthesis, where it may be rendered by
I say, now, so then, Hdt.
POSITION of δέ: properly second, being often put between the Art. and Subst., the prep. and case.

a collar, Anth.

second, δ. μετʼ ἐκεῖνον Hdt.; c. gen., δεύτερος οὐδενός

the second prize or
place, Il., Hdt.

to make to flow, shed, αἷμα Soph.

to feel the want or
loss of, be without a thing, c. gen., Il.:

c. gen. pers.
to be inferior to, Hom.

to accept or

i. e. δῆλόν [ἐστιν] ὅτι, used parenthetically,
quite clearly, manifestly, plainly, Plat., etc.

epexegetically,
that is to say, namely, Lat. scilicet, id=Plat., Xen.
to make clear, Plut.

properly,
visible, conspicuous, Il.

manifest, evident, Od.: —δῆλός εἰμι with partic., δῆλός ἐστιν ἀλγεινῶς φέρων i. e.

it is clear that they will not permit, Thuc.; also, acc. to our idiom, δῆλόν [ἐστιν] ὅτι . . , v. δηλονότι.

δῆλον itself is used like δηλαδή, as αὐτὸς πρὸς αὑτοῦ· δῆλον, all by himself,
'tis manifest, Soph.:—also, δῆλον δέ to introduce a proof, Thuc.

entry.etym:
Prob. from δῆλος, because of the legend that it became
visible by rising from the sea.
entry.sense: Delos, one of the Cyclades, birthplace of Apollo and Artemis, Od.; called also Ὀρτυγία.

intr.
to be clear or
plain, Hdt., Plat.
impers., δηλοῖ = δῆλόν ἐστι, Hdt.; fut. δηλώσει Plat.; aor1 ἐδήλωσε Xen.
